item.title: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors.Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes."These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for , told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.American voters in the communities where they’re being built They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 million of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

item.title: The World Is Prepared To Boycott Russian Hockey
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: Almost every day is a tradeoff between satisfaction and punch-bowl turds. Find a great parking spot in front of the place you want to go? There's a ticket on the windshield when you return. Good work review from the boss? Unpaid overtime the night before a holiday weekend. Winning at the card table? The last hand brings a bad beat that reallocates your winnings to someone else. When Devin Cooley received congratulations for a good game in goal for the Calgary Flames two years ago, he famously said, "Nothing's really gonna matter. We're all gonna die." Even now, he is among the most famous hockey players to non-hockey fans for that fascinating worldview. That fame, and that darkly realistic approach, didn't prevent him from getting injured last week.But Tuesday was that rarest of events—a grand day in politics. The reigning goblins got routed in nearly every way and seemingly every race, although meat slab impersonator Tommy Tuberville still won his Alabama governor's race and Mark Teixeira narrowly won his congressional race. It was great on its face, and also for all the devastated expressions that came with those losses; it is a good day when all the worst people are sad. Very nearly as satisfying, the Canadian government committed itself to a decision that made Prime Minister Mark Carney look as good as the election down here must have made him feel.Carney stood strong in the face of Canada's national addiction, hockey, to tell the Court of Arbitration for Sport to take a hike on its decision to allow Russia to play in the World Juniors Tournament that begins the day after Christmas in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta. Nearly half the 16 nations scheduled to play in the world championships in Germany in May have also said they won't participate if the Russians are allowed.

item.title: Jon Ossoff’s not-so-secret weapon against JD Vance and Marco Rubio
item.content:encoded: For more than a year, journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan had been trying — and largely failing — to raise awareness about the very strange story of Donald Trump and his aide Natalie Harp. Shortly after the 2024 election, the New York Times journalists published a profile of the lithe blonde in her early 30s, complete with photos of her gazing at Trump adoringly, explaining how she left him love letters with language like, “You are all that matters to me.” On Aug. 16, Haberman was still trying to raise the issue during an appearance on MS NOW, describing Harp as Trump’s “human binky.”But in the end, it was Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who woke up much of the public to this disturbing relationship by mentioning Harp on the campaign trail. “The defensive reaction from the White House was so over-the-top that it backfired, drawing more attention to the relationship. But a mystery remained. Haberman, Swan and many others had been talking about Harp, but it wasn’t until Ossoff said something that the White House truly lost their minds. The reaction likely had little to do with Ossoff’s comments, as elegantly as they were constructed. No, this recoil was more about the messenger than the message. At 39, Ossoff isn’t just young. He is strikingly handsome. The boyish good looks of his early career have matured into something closer to the old-fashioned allure of a 1960s-era movie star, such as Gregory Peck or Warren Beatty. Broad-chested, with great hair and a winning smile, Ossoff has a cool demeanor, good sense of humor and moral seriousness in a proportion that’s rare in politics — and that hasn’t really been seen since Barack Obama. Ossoff, in other words, can get it.Put another way, Ossoff is everything the 80-year-old president wishes he were, but isn’t. Harp’s presence is a touchy, daily reminder to both Trump and his staff of the president’s thick catalog failings as a human being. Having a young, handsome, talented man mock Trump for his emotional support aide had to have stung with a special precision. No one needs to tell the president or his staff that Ossoff feels just fine about himself — and doesn’t need a full-time emotional support aide to follow him around, praising his every move.Considering how much the White House communications staff is extremely online, they are also likely to know that Ossoff has become quite the thirst trap, even among young women and gay men who otherwise aren’t especially political on social media. As Grace Panetta of The 19th recently explained, the senator is a reliable, if unwitting, model for light-hearted crush content, much like what creators generate in tribute to movie stars like Timothée Chalamet or Tom Holland. “Take a scroll through Instagram and TikTok, and you’ll see fan edit-style videos of Ossoff Ossoff’s sex appeal doesn’t just offer a striking contrast with Trump’s oversized suits and comical combover. He’s also very different than men in the Republican ranks who are closer to his own age and, like himself, are widely seen as potential 2028 presidential candidates. At 42, Vice President JD Vance is also the subject a lot of online content. But most of it portrays him in a comically unflattering manner, with tiny dead eyes, oversized cheeks and a maniacal grin. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, 55, isn’t mocked for his looks, but he is often portrayed as a sad sack, a man too slow-witted and spineless to be much use beyond his role as Trump’s patsy. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, 46, is blessed with good looks that even three breakfast gin-and-tonics can’t take away. But with the help of Colin Jost on “Saturday Night Live,” he is mostly viewed like an overgrown frat boy crushing beer cans on his forehead. None come even close to the dreamboat treatment Ossoff receives. This disparate treatment is especially amusing because the MAGA movement has insisted for years that they are bringing back a more virile masculinity — supposedly to cure all the allegedly poisonous feminism inflicted upon America by those WNBA-loving Democrats. No doubt there are some people impressed by all the workout videos posted by MAGA leaders, though that audience probably doesn’t have much crossover with people who get second dates. But what all the chest-thumping and push-up contests of the right really communicates is overcompensation rather than reclaiming some “lost” masculinity.Beneath the right’s meltdown over Ossoff’s relatively tame comment about Harp was a molten layer of male insecurity. Steven Cheung, the volatile White House communications director, tweeted, “Jon Jackoff has to be the biggest cuck loser in politics.” White House spokesman David Ingle called the senator a “cringeworthy, feminine theatre kid.” Both unwisely lobbed these insults from X accounts featuring photos of themselves. The handy comparison left the observer to contemplate how, with MAGA, it’s typically true that every accusation is itself a confession. Similarly, Trump compared Ossoff to Pee-wee Herman, a reference to a film that is older than the senator and only served to underscore how old and out of touch the president is. MAGA’s belief that masculinity is on the decline is more a reflection of their personal fears and resentments than an accurate picture of the world. Men who can just act normal continue to do fine, or as much as one can in this economy. As with many of the thirst-trap Democrats that are rising stars, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senate hopeful Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a large part of Ossoff’s charm is that he possesses an easy masculinity, one comfortable with women’s equality. MAGA influencers may deny it, but men who actually like and respect women tend to be more attractive to women and gay men.Being chill with women’s power projects confidence. Insecure men are the ones who demand that women are forced into subservient roles, just so men can feel bigger. It speaks to an internal belief that they can’t win without cheating. That’s loser energy, not the Big Dictionary Energy being given off by Ossoff and this new crop of young, vigorous Democratic men.

item.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed
item.content:encoded: I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotels. Elevator banks. Free continental breakfast. A sad gym on the third floor where one treadmill is always busted. You know the kind of hotel I mean. The Phoenix, which opened in the 1980s at the influence of legendary rock promoter Bill Graham, is not that kind of hotel. This was a place dreamed up to serve real-deal rock stars, and to make anyone else staying there feel like part of the greater entourage.Article continues below this adAnd until early this year, it was all set to die young, as so many of its more famous guests had, Kurt Cobain chief among them. Late in 2025, b. Patisserie co-owner Michel Suas was readying to take over the Phoenix’s lot and close down the hotel permanently, presumably using the land to build some kind of overpriced but good boulangerie. But at the last second, Suas had a change of heart! HONH HONH HONH! Enter local hotelier Binoy Patel, who took the reins of the property and is keeping the hotel open. That’s right, like a phoenix rising from the ashes. You read my mind to the letter.Given this fortuitous stay of execution, my SFGATE bosses thought that I should stay at the Phoenix during my annual “Drew comes to the Bay Area for a weekand eatsway too much” trip two months ago. As a Marylander, I was ignorant to the Phoenix’s charms before booking my room. It is now my favorite hotel in the city, and if new owner Patel messes with so much as a single AC outlet in the place, he and I will have words.I didn’t expect to love the Phoenix as much as I did, certainly not at first glance. No one stays in the Tenderloin for the Tenderloin. You stay in this part of town because you have some work engagement nearby. That’s why hotelier Chip Conley founded the hotel in the first place; it was close to venues where Graham booked gigs for headline acts. Otherwise, the place is located on a nondescript, run-down stretch of Eddy Street that’s a relative desert. The hotel itself is a refurbished roadside motel, the kind of place I’d normally expect to be murdered in. The only thing shielding your room door from the rest of the world is a red iron gate to the street next to the hotel office. So my first thought before ringing the front office door was, “This place better not suck.”Article continues below this adI was buzzed by a clerk who bore more than passing resemblance to Sweetums the Muppet: a bulky, tatted-up fellow with long scraggy hair and the beard to match. Sweetums could have been the bouncer at a Hells Angels bar if he wasn’t such a sweetheart. Instead, he manned the front desk at the Phoenix and warmly offered me a number of vital pointers. I needed to use my key card at the red gate anytime I came or went, there was always free coffee in the front office if I needed it, and logging onto the hotel’s Wi-Fi required him to perform a live demo for me.“I can’t do it the usual way?” I asked Sweetums.“Doing it the usual way here is s—t,” he told me. But doing it his way worked like a charm.Article continues below this adI walked into a concrete courtyard loosely festooned with palm trees, potted succulents, and basket chairs surrounding a fat round pool. An outdoor performance stage loomed toward the back. No one was swimming in the pool when I first entered the courtyard; the water was populated exclusively by aging pool noodles, some of which had bite marks in them. But the water looked clean, which is more than you can say for the average Motel 6 pool. I crossed the courtyard to the outdoor staircase leading up to my second floor room. Standing sentry by the staircase was a huge, colorfully tiled sculpture of a frog playing the guitar. Your mother would describe this hotel as “kind of funky,” and she’d be correct.But the ultimate test for this kind of novelty hotel is your room itself. You want a hotel that’s only seedy. I’ve stayed at actual seedy hotels … the kind of hotels where s—t doesn’t work. They are not charming. So my room at the Phoenix would determine which side of the line the hotel fell on.Article continues below this adIf you’ve read this far, you won’t be surprised to learn that my room was perfect. One side of it was dominated by a floor-to-ceiling window looking out onto the courtyard, just in case any other guests wanted to watch me and a groupie going at it. Seeing as how I’ve been faithfully married for 24 years, the chances of me indulging in that particular rock star fantasy were minimal. But it was nice to know I had the option if I so chose.As for the room itself, it had everything I would have wanted from a mainstream hotel room. The bed was comfy. There were multiple charging outlets available to me, many hidden inside of retro furnishings that scanned like film props. And I didn’t need a tutorial from Sweetums on how to operate the shower or the light switches. My only beef was that the soft neon lamp hanging over my bed didn’t work, but I probably wouldn’t have used it for longer than two minutes anyway.This was a goodass hotel room, and it served as a perfect base of operations for me as I spent all week covering assignments in North Beach, Cow Hollow, Marin, Palo Alto, and elsewhere. Anytime I was slogging through my day of field reporting, I knew that my plush room at the Phoenix would be waiting for me. Best of all, when I asked Sweetums if there were any good places for breakfast nearby, he immediately told me to hit Brenda’s French Soul Food, another local institution I had been heretofore unaware of. I went to Brenda’s the following morning and ordered the bananas foster French toast, plus a breakfast sandwich. You know, for balance. I ate so well that brunch, I needed to burn some serious calories afterward.Article continues below this adAnd where better to do that than in the Phoenix pool?This was August, mind you. Temperatures in San Francisco that time of year aren’t always conducive to pool days, so I suited up with the mercury hovering around a crisp 65 in the hotel’s courtyard. I fully expected the water to be even colder than that, so imagine my surprise when I jumped off the edge and KERSPLOOSH! Suddenly I was warmer and happier than I’d been all trip. The Phoenix pool isn’t so hot as to feel gross, it’s just well calibrated for a warm swim in a city that wants you to slowly freeze to death. Once in the pool, I knew immediately that leaving the pool would render me a pile of chattering teeth. So I grabbed one of the chewed-up pool noodles and lounged to my big fat heart’s content.Article continues below this adI felt no danger from the dirty street outside, nor did I feel embarrassed to be a 49-year-old man, rash guard and all, swimming all by himself in the middle of a random weekday. I know that Sweetums was standing sentry at the front desk, and I knew that I was exactly where I wanted to be: kicking back in the heart of one of the best cities in the world, with not a single worry on my mind. If that’s not the life of a rock star, I don’t know what is.

item.title: And Take Your Stupid Hat, Too!
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: Haley Stevens was not on the ballot in Michigan, because the outgoing House rep had already lost her Senate bid in the Democratic primary back in August. But with a sudden burst of ineptitude reminiscent of the 2000s Detroit Lions, she found a novel way to lose on Tuesday.The 43-year-old from the suburbs—clearly still raw from the fact that Abdul El-Sayed beat her despite all her money, perhaps also mind-alteringly horny for her fiance Jason Turkish—made a shock endorsement of the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers, at the 11th hour. This choice, the logic of which Stevens could not articulate even given many chances, made her as welcome among Democrats as Ron Artest at a Pistons home game. It also paid off about as well as the Tigers' 2017 Justin Verlander trade, with El-Sayed beating Rogers like Michigan basketball beat UConn. Haley Stevens in 2026 has officially tied the '08 Lions' record for fewest wins in a year: zero.To close her multi-day display of bizarre vindictiveness and sudden paranoia, Stevens made a decision that's especially easy to laugh about: the hat. While trying not to bump into her mother on the sidewalk on their way to vote, Stevens spoke into the news camera about—I don't know, probably stickin' it to 'em or something. I was too distracted to listen, owing to her humongous beige headgear.

item.title: In The Dream House, With Tom Krell
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Before I tell you what Harry and I talked about with the great Tom Krell (of How to Dress Well) for the first 95 percent of this week's episode of , I have to start with an ask based in what we talked about in the last five percent: our quest to get Tom to sing the national anthem before a Denver Nuggets game. He's sent in several tapes, rocking what he's described as an interesting balance of falsetto and regular-style singing, but the Nuggets have yet to book him. If you work for the Nuggets or know anyone who works for the Nuggets, please, we need your help putting our boy on. You know he's got the voice for it!Anyway, other topics discussed include James Cameron coming up with the idea for in a dream; the issue of whether Nikola Jokic is washed; guys who move weird with the ball; my new haircut; the work of German philosopher Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi; the concept of Keaton Wagler having snakes in his boots; the real issues with David Adelman's leadership style; and watching NBA games on your phone on mute at 1.1x speed while mildly drunk and trying not to wake your dog, wife, or baby. It's a real banger.

item.title: House Margins
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: NBC News currently projects that Democrats will hold 258 seats in the House in the next Congress — an 81-seat margin. Let’s assume that’s accurate; in any case, it won’t be far off. If that holds, that will be the largest majority either party has held since 1990 — 36 years ago. It’s important to note that this was in the pre-1994 U.S. political system in which Democrats still held large majorities based in part on incumbency in southern districts that were already strongly Republican. That changed decisively in 1994, and U.S. politics has never been the same. The last time Republicans won a majority that large was, I believe, in 1928.

item.title: If You’re Going To Change Your School’s Mascot, At Least Have The Decency To Get Weird
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: The University of San Francisco is a staid enclave of higher learning, a rectangular hodgepodge of buildings gerrymandered to fill 19 square blocks of prime city real estate. It is a culturally and ethnically diverse educational operation and has been so for decades. Also, it has no football team to interfere with the peace and quiet of the place, and its men's basketball team has not been of national consequence in 45 years. In other words, it minds its business. So far, so good.So it came as a bit of a jar when the school decided last Friday to change its mascot from a cartoon Spanish don—his name is Don Francisco, and he has both the requisite outsized biceps and a jaunty pencil-thin mustache of the kind last worn by Ronald Colman seven decades ago—to a wolf, an animal which is not particularly indigenous to any part of the city, save maybe the Financial District. Even then they could have just gone with Rapacious Bastards and sold a few more T-shirts when they roll out the new mascot next spring.It has taken four years to implement this move, which began with a student government proposal to ditch the mascot in 2022. That became a petition signed by approximately 400 students, who correctly viewed the mascot as a representation of the Spanish colonization/brutalization of the indigenous population four centuries ago. All good, there; the student body should be the deciding vote on anything on campus that impacts mostly students. It's their house, after all.

item.title: A Glorious Night: Bask in America’s Own Redemption
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: A lot of things happened. Here are some of the things. This is TPM’s Morning Memo.Behold the New U.S. Political MapWow. It’s impossible to get my head around the sweeping changes to the map coming out of last night. It’s going to take few days to process it all. Just wow.The final totals in the House and Senate aren’t in yet and might not be known for several more days, but as it stands now, the outcome leaves Democrats with congressional majorities that look a lot like what they won in the 2008 election that swept Barack Obama into office in the aftermath of another unpopular Middle East war.The NYT is projecting that Democrats will wind up with 55 Senate seats and 258 seats in the House. After the 2008 election, Democrats had 56 Senate seats and 257 House seats. (This is never a perfect comparison because the numbers fluctuate throughout each Congress, with deaths, party switches, etc.) But that only tells part of the story.What about the sheer gain of 10 Senate seats? Republicans picked up 10 Senate seats in the 1994 election, but Democrats haven’t added that many seats since they picked up 15 seats in the 1958 election, the beginning of a Democratic Senate majority that would last until the 1980 election.And the gain of 42 House seats? You don’t have to go that far back: Democrats picked up 41 seats in the 2020 election.But matching the size of Democratic majority after 2008 — ±257 seats — means equalling the high water mark for Democrats since the 1994 election, the seminal election which ended their 42-year House majority. To put it in the context of our current politics, this Democratic majority will be significantly bigger than any recent Republican majority. The GOP high water mark in the House in the modern era was 247 seats after the 2014 election.With the results still coming in, this isn’t about pinpointing which records have been set yet, but just about giving you some sense of the historic comps.Beyond the Senate and House, entire states turned completely blue, with statehouse trifectas (governor plus control of both legislative chambers) in:Democrats broke statehouse trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas. They will hold a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years.: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan: Keisha Lance Bottoms in GeorgiaNative American female governor: Deb Haaland in New Mexico: Chris Pappas in New HampshireBiggest Upset of the Night:Biggest Wow of the Night: TexasThe dual toxicity of Donald Trump and Ken Paxton finally brought a blue wave to Texas that had been nearly 30 years in the making. Gone in one fell swoop are:Attorney General Ken PaxtonThe View from Across the PondBBC: Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump’s RepublicansThe Independent: Trump told Americans to ‘pretend I’m on the ballot.’ They did — and voted against him: Regardless of what happens, an amazing showing by Scott Colom.: A lot still to be figured out, especially with ranked-choice voting.From the GOP Insider Perspective …The inside-the-beltway pubs framed last night’s result in GOP terms, as they usually do:We’ve had some fluky elections in the past 20 years, where Republicans in particular have fielded bad candidates or where the timing of vacancies has created outlier results. But this was so broad-based that there was nothing fluky about it.I look in particular at the Senate races across the South: South Carolina, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, and Louisiana. Even the losing Democratic candidates had remarkably strong performances. The groundswell was nationwide.What Didn’t Happen: No CoupingElection interference spearheaded by the Trump DOJ in the weeks and months before the election was an unprecedented abuse of the powers of the federal government to undermine free and fair elections to try to preserve the power of the president’s party in Congress.But it started to become apparent late last week that there was no master plan or strategy for Main Justice that went beyond a relatively meager effort to use the Big Lie of rampant noncitizen voting as a pretext for contesting California elections. But even that largely fell apart by Election Day. The separate effort to block certification of the Senate race in Alaska (where the other Dan Sullivan is on track to finish FOURTH) was its own particular weirdness.What remained unknown was whether the White House had its own plan for more sweeping and direct election interference through sheer use of force. In the end, nothing along those lines materialized at all.I ran through two different checklists on Monday of different levels of election interference to look for on Election Day and essentially none of that came to pass. The third act of the play — the post-election period — was ripe for Trump-driven chaos if there were a lot of close races and control of the House and/or Senate hung in the balance. The Democratic sweep took that off table.America will always break your heart but then find a way to redeem herself.There remains an enormous amount of work ahead. The immediate work is to contain Trump for two more years. That is essential work, and it won’t necessarily yield decisive, crowd-pleasing outcomes like impeachment or criminal convictions or other much-needed public forms of accountability. But that doesn’t mean it can’t be effective politically beneficial. Regardless, it is absolutely necessary.Coming into the election, I thought containing Trump was the best we could hope for — and frankly that public expectations among Trump foes were too high for what could be done beyond that. Rebuilding and reforming would have to come after winning the White House in 2028.But the Democratic gains at the state level open up new avenues to begin some of the forward-looking work sooner: starting to repair the colossal damage Trump has inflicted, rebuilding civil society, enlarging and enriching public life in America, reforming a weakened political system that Trump was able to exploit.All of those efforts can start now at the state level and set the stage for what can happened federally if and when Democrats control the White House and congressional majorities. It’s a chance for a flourishing of new kind of politics, reforms, initiatives, and approaches. See what works and apply it nationally.But … having a firm new grasp on the levers of power does not in itself fundamentally change America.The ingredients that led to Trump all remain: a broken information ecosystem; a virtually unrestricted campaign finance system; unsustainable levels of economic inequality and wealth concentration; and an emptiness at the heart of American political life. Perhaps worst of all, one of the two major political parties has abandoned democracy.After the disaster of Trump’s second election, I wrote that this is no longer merely a political problem but a cultural one. Politics can only do so much. The greatest danger in MAGA’s authoritarian impulses was its abuse of the power of government to dictate culture: white, Christian, native born, intolerant, militaristic, and male dominant. It was the most perverse possible response to the existential threats of climate change and AI.Regaining power doesn’t reclaim culture, but it’s a heck of a start.

item.title: A college reading list from 1966
item.author: Minnesotastan
item.content:encoded: Nicholas Dames has taught Literature Humanities, Columbia University’s required great-books course, since 1998. He loves the job, but it has changed. Over the past decade, students have become overwhelmed by the reading. College kids have never read everything they’re assigned, of course, but this feels different. Dames’s students now seem bewildered by the thought of finishing multiple books a semester. His colleagues have noticed the same problem. Many students no longer arrive at college—even at highly selective, elite colleges—prepared to read books.This development puzzled Dames until one day during the fall 2022 semester, when a first-year student came to his office hours to share how challenging she had found the early assignments. Lit Hum often requires students to read a book, sometimes a very long and dense one, in just a week or two. But the student told Dames that, at her public high school, she had never been required to read an entire book. She had been assigned excerpts, poetry, and news articles, but not a single book cover to cover...Twenty years ago, Dames’s classes had no problem engaging in sophisticated discussions of one week and the next. Now his students tell him up front that the reading load feels impossible. It’s not just the frenetic pace; they struggle to attend to small details while keeping track of the overall plot...In 1976, about 40 percent of high-school seniors said they had read at least six books for fun in the previous year, compared with 11.5 percent who hadn’t read any. By 2022, those percentages had flipped...Carol Jago, a literacy expert who crisscrosses the country helping teachers design curricula, says that educators tell her they’ve stopped teaching the novels they’ve long revered, such as and . The pandemic, which scrambled syllabi and moved coursework online, accelerated the shift away from teaching complete works... At the prep school that I graduated from five years ago, I took a Jane Austen course my senior year. I read only a single Austen novel...Some experts I spoke with attributed the decline of book reading to a shift in values rather than in skill sets. Students can still read books, they argue—they’re just choosing not to.Students today are far more concerned about their job prospects than they were in the past. Every year, they tell Howley that, despite enjoying what they learned in Lit Hum, they plan to instead get a degree in something more useful for their career...For years, Dames has asked his first-years [university] about their favorite book. In the past, they cited books such as and . Now, he says, almost half of them cite young-adult books. Rick Riordan’s Percy Jackson series seems to be a particular favorite...

item.title: Democrats, fuck yeah!
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Loyal and patriotic citizens, please stand by for a message of the utmost importance from the President of the United States, Supreme Ruler of the Western Hemisphere, Lord-Emperor of the Sky Above and All the Planets, Conqueror Of Every War, God’s Own Avatar on Earth, Grand Re-namer of Water, and the Dumbest Fucking Imbecile to Ever Shit Himself Raw In the Oval Bordello.“I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP”Oh, come off it, you tiresome crybaby. How many times did this repulsive dipshit tell everyone to pretend that was on the ballot? According to the WaPo, it was at least 41 times over the past couple of weeks. Yeah, well, guess what, Nimrod — everyone vote as if you were on that ballot of theirs. Don’t go to us if you don’t like the results.You shit your bed. Now go lie in it.(Folks, I’m running on way too much caffeine and way too little sleep this morning. I’m going to jot down a couple of quick hits and then maybe toddle back to bed.)Well, we did it. We ran the table, and flipped both the House and the Senate back to Democratic control.Now we can begin to dismantle this whole wretched experiment in what would happen if we took a greedy moron, put him in charge of an entire country, and let him to whatever the fuck he wants.Yesterday, almost all the heroes who were supposed to win, did. Among them were James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa in Texas. Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayad, who becomes the first Muslim in the Senate.And almost all the shitbags who supposed to lose, lost. The rank, amateurs, like Darline Graham. The malodorous, what-the-fuck-is-he-even-doing-here political tourists, like Vivek Ramaswamy. The low-wattage corruption-factories like Ken Paxton, who couldn’t even articulate a reason for running, beyond And, most deliciously, that useless lump of protoplasm up in Maine, the one who’d spent thirty years doing fuck-all, apart from collecting a paycheck. I wonder what Susan Collins will do next? I’m really concerned, aren’t you?BANGOR, Maine — Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) greeted supporters at her election party throughout the night but was a no-show after losing her bid for a sixth term.Her campaign played Semisonic’s “Closing Time” and began packing up the room without any concession speech from Collins.Oh, and I regret that I must inform you that Jon Husted’s impossibly-sculpted ass — that big, strong gluteus, with tears in its eyes — lost its bid for reelection, too.The whole country is mad at the GOP right now. Here’s just one measure of how pissed off: the last time Kansas elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Republicans have no one to blame but themselves. They really take a greedy moron, put him in charge of an entire country, and let him do whatever the fuck he wanted to.Then they stepped back and completely abdicated their Constitutionally-mandated role to act as a check against dumbfuckery. Whatever the moron wanted, that was fine with then. Incoherent tariffs? Go for it, Dear Leader. Unconstitutional executive orders? You do you, bro. Fire all the experts and replace them with morons? Sounds good to us. Prosecute political enemies? Knock yourself out. Send masked thugs to disappear people off the streets, and shoot anyone they want? Sure, why not? Kick millions of people off their healthcare so that gazillionaires can have another tax cut? Have at it. Bulldoze half the White House to rubble and replace it with some farkakte dance hall? Fucking go nuts. Wage illegal wars and alienate all our allies? What could possibly go wrong?And look what happened. The moron broke our entire fucking country. The whole thing! Do you know how hard it is to break a country the size of America? It’s like trying to bankrupt a casino. People thought was impossible, until Donny came along.Do you know how badly you have to fuck up to get Republicans to vote for Democrats? And now the grown-ups have to come in and fix all that shit. I better not hear one complaint about how much it’s costing or how much time it’s taking. Don’t make me come over there and explain just how much stuff is broken.That’s Rep. Robert Garcia, the Democrat who is now the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee. He posted that last night, after winning his own reelection.He’s talking to you, Donny. And you, Piss-Drunk Pete Kegstand. You too, Bobby Brainworms. Don’t pretend you can’t hear him over the noise of that whale-head-separating chainsaw. He’s talking to all of you White House shitweasels.Lawyer the fuck up. Accountability is coming.Hey — I know what would be fun right about now. Let’s overdose on schadenfreude while watching MAGA completely lose their shit on Elon’s Nazi Bar.I’m going to give the final word today to Mister Barack HUSSEIN Obama, because he’s so good at being gracious. Me, I at grace.Tonight, the American people sent a clear message — they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face. These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country — including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first. We also owe a debt of gratitude to the thousands of election officials and volunteers from both parties who helped ensure a smooth election and carried out one of the most essential functions of our democracy. While this administration has another two years in office, our job now is to roll up our sleeves, make changes wherever we have the power to do so, prevent further damage, and lay the groundwork for the future.He really is so truly good at this. As I keep saying, I think this kid’s going to have a real future in front of him, some day.And isn’t in nice that, at least this one time, we all get a puppy — as opposed to, y’know, ?Not just a puppy, but a Daily Claudia, too.Let’s do some random selfies. Here’s Half Moon in Dobbs Ferry on April 15, 2025.In the car on January 17, 2025.And a very special shout-out to my friend Sam, who texted the following to me at 11:30 last night.Have a great Wednesday, everyone. here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: How To Build a Human Tower
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: People will turn any activity into a competition. For hundreds of years, the people of Catalonia have built human towers by climbing onto each other's shoulders in a stunt called castell. Of course they've developed competitions for the highest tower, held during festivals. These were for men only until the 1980s, but with the addition of women, the towers can now reach nine or ten levels high.It's a matter of strength, agility, numbers, and physics. The strongest people are arranged at the bottom in a precisely-calculated formation to build a sturdy, stable base. The middle layers rely on balance or else the tower will fall. The top climbers are lightweight and fearless, often children. BBC Earth Science brings us this clip from the TV series Forces of Nature to show us how these human towers are built. Yes, sometimes they do collapse, although the participants are trained for it, and the bottom layer serves as a cushion for falling bodies. And they are all barefoot to reduce injury. Still, these competitions have ambulances standing by in case they are needed. (via Laughing Squid)

item.title: Event Invite: Can AI help nonprofits fundraise?
Goddamn, That Was Satisfying
item.author: Barry Petchesky
item.content:encoded: It started quickly, with Georgia's Senate race being called for Jon Ossoff 18 minutes after polls closed, and never let up. One by one, precincts returned blue. The map was bluer than you've ever seen. Places went blue that haven't gone blue in a lifetime. It was bluer than a Lenny Bruce set. By the time it was called in Michigan for Abdul El-Sayed at 1:00 a.m. ET and Steve Kornacki was propofol'd and dragged off air for the night, both the House and the Senate were firmly in the hands of the Democrats, a blue wave not seen since the post-Watergate midterms of 1974, and for many of the same reasons.If a race held any uncertainty, it broke left. The long-held dream of blue Texas is here, and resoundingly. The North Carolina House, redistricted last year by Republicans to safely go 11-3 in their favor, is going to end up something like 10-4 Dems. Washington, D.C., elected a democratic socialist mayor. Michigan elected the nation's first Muslim Senator, New Hampshire our first openly gay man. It is hard to overstate how complete and far-reaching this blue tsunami was. Alabama elected a transgender woman to the House. One Maryland county's Democratic candidate for sheriff barely campaigned—he says he hates public speaking, and bought no ads—and won.Democrats largely stayed on message and campaigned smartly on the real things people care about—the economy—but that Maryland sheriff race best illustrates what was actually being voted on. This was a nationwide referendum, on Republican rule and on Donald Trump. And it turns out that while voters may be prone to touching a hot stove, they will not keep their hands on the burner for ever.

item.title: ‘There Is One Fight’: American Voters Reject Tech Oligarchy
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Last month, OpenAI CEO that “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” referring to ChatGPT users dying, people losing their jobs to AI, and the other negative externalities we have seen from AI. Altman wasn’t running for office Tuesday. But this worldview—that the masses must shut up and suffer while oligarchs centralize power, self-deal, spend wildly to capture the political process, and automate away human endeavors so they can amass yet more wealth—was wholly repudiated in Tuesday’s election as people in Red States, Blue States, and Purple States rejected the cruelty, corruption, and depravity economy we’ve seen over the last few years. They are tired of kleptocracy. The main difference between Donald Trump’s administration this term and his first term is that Silicon Valley’s oligarchs have lined up to kiss the ring; look no further than the photos from his inauguration and his gilded gala with China’s President Xi Jinping earlier this fall. Every major tech company CEO has spent the last two years flattering Trump, giving him gifts, and trying to capture the political process. They have been generously rewarded for their fealty and their money as the Trump administration has spent the last two years letting Big Tech do whatever it wants. Elon Musk was given the keys to the federal government and used them to slash critical government programs, lay off tens of thousands of public servants, and replace collective human expertise with and . His companies have continued to rake in billions in government contracts, his busted AI has been integrated into critical government systems, and the cuts led by his “Department of Government Efficiency” has, conservatively, killed many thousands of people around the world. Trump has pardoned crypto criminals, his family has made billions of dollars in cryptocurrency scams, and has overseen the rise of a gambling and prediction market-based “economy” rife with insider trading and misery (the idea of the administration doing anything to crack down on this is so implausible that to even suggest it could happen is laughable). He has installed manosphere podcasters, X trolls, and conspiracy theorists into top administration roles; they have performed even worse than their already low expectations. He has leveraged commercial surveillance companies to build a brutal, tech-powered mass deportation campaign. His government’s communications strategy can be described in no other way than inscrutable AI slop shitposting. This is to say nothing of the cost of living crisis Trump has caused as he’s started an illegal war in Iran that has driven up gas and diesel prices and levied tariffs on America’s allies for reasons that defy explanation. This has driven up the price of everything even as Trump’s administration slashes regulations on fossil fuel companies and big corporations. And then there’s AI. The Trump administration has let Sam Altman, Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, and Satya Nadella do whatever they want, even as their products drive mass anxiety, the destruction of the internet as we know it, and have caused corporations to bet that the future is widespread mass unemployment. Trump has cheered on the construction of data centers even as his base of supporters have said they don’t want them in their communities. Trump has said American communities should and that if communities “want to be successful and rich” they should build more data centers. As a reward for letting Silicon Valley run the country, Elon Musk spent $474 million trying to help Republicans maintain the status quo; super PACs tied to the cryptocurrency and artificial intelligence industries spent roughly $250 million to largely support Republicans and oppose Democrats, according to Molly White’s Tech Influence Watch project. A16z and people tied to it spent roughly $94.4 million trying to influence the election, according to White. This is just a small sample of the ways that Silicon Valley attempted to put its thumbs on the scale of this election to prop up a deeply unpopular administration. And, in nearly every conceivable way, voters aggressively rejected Trump and Silicon Valley’s vision for America. It turns out people do not want to accept “some bad things happening” to pad the valuations and pocketbooks of billionaires and trillionaires when the “bad things” include worsening wealth inequality, a housing and cost of living crisis, mass automation and unemployment, mass surveillance, cuts to government services, foreign wars, loud, polluting data centers that employ a few construction workers while they’re being built and no one after that are being used to increase profits for out-of-state corporations, and a culture war that infringes on the civil rights of immigrants and trans people.This was a rejection of Trump and the Republican Party, but also a rejection of big tech. Across the country, there were 40 ballot measures about AI data center projects; voters chose to restrict 39 of them. In Ohio—a state that has become extremely Red in recent cycles—Democrat Sherrod Brown cruised to a five-point win running on a campaign to rein in data centers. Vivek Ramaswamy, a Peter Thiel acolyte and billionaire venture capitalist was absolutely trounced by Amy Acton, a public health official who supports data center moratoriums and vaccines and presented herself to the state’s voters as being a normal person and not a deranged Twitter troll. In New York State, Governor Kathy Hochul won reelection after enacting the nation’s first statewide moratorium on new hyperscale data centers in July; her opponent called the moratorium “crazy” and vowed to end it if he won. In Texas, Musk spent $212 million trying to elect the wildly unpopular Ken Paxton (who, as an aside, once 404 Media’s reporting); in exchange for lighting this money on fire, Texas has, in James Talarico, its first Democratic Senator in nearly 40 years. Talarico began his campaign by saying “The people at the top — the Elon Musks, the Rupert Murdochs, the Mark Zuckerbergs of the world — they spend so much time and energy keeping us angry and divided because our unity is a threat to their wealth and their power.” Musk barely tweeted Tuesday; once it became clear his preferred candidates had lost and that people do not want AI data centers, “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” presumably because it’s clear people don’t want them here on Earth. Jason Calacanis, the intolerable venture capitalist and host of the unlistenable All In podcast tweeted a bunch of prediction market screenshots of the Talarico race and said he “never expected Texas to turn blue. Ugh, I moved here to get away from the left lunacy!” "Silicon Valley billionaires want us to believe that Al robots will destroy humanity," Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said recently. "But the biggest threat to humanity are the tech oligarchs themselves."Silicon Valley spent wildly on the election and Republicans have spent much of the last decade trying to press structural advantages to gerrymander districts, suppress the vote, and sow doubt on our elections. The sheer anger voters feel was enough to overwhelm these efforts Tuesday, nearly without exception (the one main outlier: A billionaire wealth tax ballot measure in California looks likely to fail after billionaires spent $379 million lobbying to kill it, outspending the opposition 250-to-1, with many billionaires threatening to move their companies and themselves out of the state). Given this, it should not be taken for granted that elections can or will always go this way, and Democrats need to show that they are not scared of governing.Up and down the ballot, in all states, voters were generally given the choice between largely normal people trying to fight for the working class and sycophantic cartoon supervillains, nepo picks, fumbling buffoons, and Twitter trolls seeking to enable the regime and Big Tech’s vision of the future, where AI CEOs become trillionaires and everyone else loses their job to a robot and breathes methane gas from the data centers in their backyards. It turns out that from Michigan to Mississippi (), people are done accepting “bad things happening” for the benefits of the richest people in the world. Nominally, there were a lot of issues at play in this election, but there is, really, only one issue. There is a vision of the world focused on improving the wellbeing of average people and there is a vision of the world that focused on making a few dozen people in Silicon Valley and Washington, D.C. even richer and more powerful. Newly-elected Texas Democratic Gov (!?!?) Gina Hinojosa to the , which still doesn’t get it.Hinojosa crushed three-term incumbent governor Greg Abbott by running as an “economic populist,” a label the media has wrongly given to Trump and MAGA because they villainize immigrants and trans people but govern like oligarchs. “We are facing an existential crisis in this country because tech giants are having their way with us,” Hinojosa recently told the who, like normal, had fully missed the point. “There is one fight,” she added, referring to the people vs the oligarchs. Now, Democrats need to govern like it.

item.title: jjfx
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: jjfx is a terminal interface for managing Jujutsu workspaces and the agents working in them inside of the terminal.This tool's workspace list groups work by status and opens a commit graph or the selected workspace's diff. Keyboard actions create and remove workspaces, fetch changes, rebase work and resolve conflicts. A worker pool dispatches tickets or written tasks to agents in separate workspaces.jjfx exposes commands for dispatch, review and delivery, with JSON status output for scripts. Dispatch avoids workspaces already open in a terminal and refuses uncertain cases unless forced.This too is best used by developers that are using Jujutsu who want to review parallel changes and coordinate with agent work across multiple workspaces.

item.title: bootvine
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: bootvine is a terminal tool that shows which systemd startup services are being initialized in the Linux system after startup and shutdown.It shows a live tree timeline of which services are still starting and what they are currently waiting for. The timeline gives details of which services took the longest (in seconds) or failed and which ones appear with their error messages and recent logs.The tree shows services which belong at which stage of the loading process and it gives a short description of what the service does. bootvine is runs on Linux systems that use systemd and can show the earliest stage of startup if that stage uses systemd too.bootvine is very useful to Linux users who want to find out which systemd services are delaying startup or shutdown, see what those services are waiting for and to easily investigate why something fails without scrolling through the kernel and systemd logs.

item.title: rail
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: rail is a terminal email client for reading and sending mail through Gmail and Microsoft 365.It combines accounts in one inbox and keeps messages in a local SQLite store for reading and searching. It also supports saved searches, snoozing and bulk actions, so several conversations can be archived, moved or marked as read together.Messages are written in your preferred editor, then reviewed with their attachments before sending. Drafts stay on your computer until you choose to save them to your account, and a ten-second delay gives you time to cancel a send.rail runs on Linux and macOS and is for developers and system administrators who prefer managing personal and work email alongside their other terminal tools.

item.title: jotter
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: jotter is a terminal-based Jupyter notebook editor that can run notebooks and renders LaTeX math formulas and plots in your terminal.It can open regular Jupyter notboook files (.ipynb) and after running code in the notebook, it displays its output and supports displaying inline LaTeX formulas drawn as Kitty Graphics, Sixel or iTerm2 image format depending on your terminal. It can also display inline animated matplotlib figures and renders are designed to have fast feedback loops.Notebook edits are auto-saved and jotter's editor deals with crash recovery which protects unsaved edits to pick up where you left off. Vim key-bindings are supported in the editor (if you are familiar with Vim mode navigation) and you can also use jotter to load from any virtualenv setup.This tool is very useful towards students, machine learning developers, researchers or anyone looking for alternative Jupyter notebook editors that can open full notebooks and inspect their live results in of a terminal with inline fast rendering.

item.title: tennis
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: tennis is a command-line tool that displays CSV or TSV and other structured data in the form of formatted terminal tables.The columns can be auto-resized to fit the terminal dimensions and it truncates long cells and formats numeric values. It can be customized in how it displays the data such as choosing the colors to match the background or the border styles.tennis can also be used as a CLI and accepts JSON, JSONL and SQLite data as input alongside other delimited files. It has a peak mode to summarize the data shape and column contents if you prefer to avoid viewing all the data in one table.This terminal tool is useful to developers who need an alternative CSV viewer that is cross platform, can inspect beyond CSV files and is composable via piping command output for automation.

item.title: rmlint
item.author: Curator
item.content:encoded: rmlint is a command-line tool that scans directories for duplicate files and other filesystem files.It compares file contents to identify duplicates, with filters for size and modification time. It can find files that are empty, have broken symbolic links or files that have invalid ownership permissions.By default, a scan leaves the scanned files untouched and writes a shell script for review. You can choose which copies to keep and configure the script to delete duplicates or replace them with hard links or symbolic links. It can deal with caching so that it saves time in searching again until there is a difference in the file.rmlint is for users such as system administrators, developers and archivists who need a tool to reclaiming space and find duplicate files in large file collections or checking an old backup drive for files already stored elsewhere.

item.title: Blue By You
item.author: Dave Pell
item.source: NextDraft: The Day's Most Fascinating News
item.content:encoded: You’d be forgiven for assuming I used AI to write this post. After years of suffering from electile dysfunction, I’m hardly trained in the art of writing positive political stories. But I’m not sure AI could handle this task either. Even after solving for some of the most convoluted equations, it’s not clear that we have enough data center number-crunching computing power online to fully measure the scope of the blue wave that Democrats just surfed from the redwood forest to the Reflecting Pool waters. Even some of the deepest red districts were somehow left tangled up in blue, as the Dems took the House and Senate by margins, and in places, that stunned even the most optimistic prognosticators. For two years, the traditional corporations didn’t stand up for democracy. Big tech didn’t stand up for democracy. The powerful didn’t stand up for democracy. The people stood. Stood up against corruption, cruelty, cowardice and cluelessness, in a complete repudiation of Trumpism; one so sweeping that even the election denier in chief has to accept the results. So to those who stood — from the streets of Minneapolis to courtrooms across America to campaign war rooms to voting lines in towns where the unthinkable was achieved — I mean it when I say: Thank you for your attention to this matter.+ Knock, Knock. Blue’s there. That’s it. That’s the whole joke. The shift in voting patterns was so dramatic, it’s all you need. (Gift Article): How Americans Voted in 2026. (The exit polls suggested people knew dumb had a b at the end.)+ “Trump has been forced to face his political mortality. He asked voters to make these midterm elections a referendum on him, to imagine that his name was on the ballot. They listened—and then rejected him. It is a stunning, widespread rebuke.” Jonathan Lemire in (Gift Article): Repudiation. And from Helen Lewis in (Gift Article): A Night of Pure Trumpenfreude. “In the end, not even Jon Husted’s phenomenal ass was enough to save the Republicans. Nor Elon Musk’s $500 million in campaign donations. Nor those helpful visual aids showing the great improvement in the caulking of the Reflecting Pool.” (Trump is still dangerous as hell, but less so, and there’s electoral light at the end of the tunnel.)+ After telling voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” at least 47 times, Trump is trying to pretend this wasn’t about him. “I wasn’t on the ticket, and because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote.” Not even Natalie Harp’s printer believes that at this point. I guess that’s why they call it the blues…While Texas is hardly the reddest place to go blue, they felt the dramatic voting shift there in Texas-sized proportions. “Texas’ governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general and every other statewide candidate fell, upending the state’s political power structure in one night.” : Democrats seize power in Texas, ending decades of GOP dominance. This shellacking follows years of particularly cruel and occasionally tragic attacks on women’s health. Let’s hope those policies change as quickly as the political winds they stirred.“Here are a few things $474 million can buy: roughly 77 million Big Macs, about 12,814 Tesla Model 3s, or approximately 2,724 years of a U.S. senator’s average salary. If you’re Elon Musk, it could also buy you one deeply disappointing evening in November.” $500 Million Bought Elon Nothing. (It also basically amounts to nothing for him.)+ “Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections, especially in his home state of Texas. After Democrats won sweeping victories in the midterm elections, gaining control of both houses of Congress and capturing other important state races, shares of SpaceX and Tesla, which are both run by Mr. Musk, fell sharply on Wednesday.” Elon lost big. But I wouldn’t worry about him. The money he spent was a rounding error. There’s a bigger story here, though. We’ve learned that money alone, especially when it comes from a largely despised source, doesn’t win elections. Thankfully, neither does gerrymandering.“What is your favorite way to spend an evening? … Last year, when more than 2,000 survey participants answered this open-ended query, many of them described a very different kind of scene: a night at home, cozied up with family. When researchers analyzed the long answers, they found that 43 percent of respondents mentioned time with family or a romantic partner—the most common activity, tied with watching a TV show.” (This was exactly how my wife and I spent our evenings, until we watched all of TV. Now we’re in a holding pattern.) The Socializing That’s Replacing Friend Time. “Combining Hinojosa’s victory with those of other Democrats who won gubernatorial races from Georgia to Ohio and Pennsylvania could leave half of proposed AI data center additions across the US vulnerable to stricter local scrutiny and pushback. All of them made more aggressive data center regulation a central part of their campaigns.” (Gift Article): AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout. And from : Americans Really Don’t Like Data Centers.+ There are still many races in play. Democrat Scott Colom leads the Mississippi Senate race by 43 votes against Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Colom having a chance in Mississippi was on exactly no one’s bingo card.) Plus, Navy admiral fired by Hegseth flips Mace’s South Carolina seat. By the time she’s sworn in for her job, he may be out of his.+ The market seems to like the election results. Bigly.+ “Thanat Tantinam, a colorectal surgeon in Thailand, knows a lot of things from his medical training, like the ins and outs of the human digestive system, or bowel cancer rates. But also: Never eat Kentucky Fried Chicken at work. Since he was a medical student, around a decade ago, the American fast food franchise has been the subject of an odd superstition among Thai doctors, many of whom believe that eating its chicken at work will lead to intolerably busy shifts.” (Gift Article): Why Doctors in Thailand Fear KFC.

item.title: The most dangerous days start now
item.author: 1axblm1cumu2y3nl0g0xm7ic7vu4e4cdm8576b@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
item.content:encoded: I was up late last night poring over results and dealing with last-minute legal issues. My staff told me that the paywall for my exclusive content was set to go back up today, but I insisted we keep it down until the end of the week. There is simply too much at stake.I was a lawyer at Democratic headquarters in 1994, when Republicans gained control of the House for the first time in 40 years. I was there when Barack Obama swept into office and brought with him a 60-seat majority in the Senate and 257 seats in the House.Yet in some respects, what we saw last night was even more dramatic.Democrats did not just recapture both chambers. They did it by winning seats that Republicans gerrymandered last year to prevent exactly this result, and by winning in states Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.Those gerrymanders backfired, pushing even more seats into the Democrats’ column. Trump’s historic unpopularity hung around Republicans’ necks and lifted Democrats.But amid all the joy and celebration, we must not forget that this election was held in the shadow of Trump’s relentless assault on voting. Over the past two years, he has issued executive orders limiting voting and tried to enact new voter suppression laws.At the tip of the spear has been the Department of Justice. Under Attorney General Todd Blanche, it has prosecuted Trump’s political opponents. It has threatened election officials for refusing to disregard state election laws.The DOJ has sued and sued, and lost and lost. Its record in voting and election cases is two wins and 31 losses. And it is not done.Ballots are still being counted, and important races have yet to be called. As I have said before, the most dangerous period in any election is the days immediately after it.That is when, in 2020, Trump began his barrage of lawsuits. It is when the Big Lie was born.Last night, as the returns came in and the shape of the night became clear, Weijia Jiang, CBS News’ White House correspondent, posted on social media that “the president is watching returns with cabinet members, senior staff, and advisors tonight…. Trump is not planning to push officials not to certify results or declare martial law, but they will be checking for irregularities.”That is how far we have fallen. That is how dangerous a moment we are in.For weeks, I have warned that we are in the midst of a constitutional crisis. The fact that a network reporter felt the need to confirm that Trump will not try to block certification or declare martial law shows how close we have come to losing our democracy.In the days ahead, I expect my law firm will be fighting to ensure that every lawful vote is counted and that Democratic candidates prevail. We will no doubt find ourselves in court against Republican lawyers and the DOJ.These fights won’t affect control of Congress, but they will determine how much room Democrats have to maneuver in both chambers. They will also set the stage for real oversight of, and accountability for, a president who has so far operated without either.But the fights in court will be only part of the story. Trump used his 2020 defeat to build a movement around the Big Lie of election denial. He will no doubt try to do the same now.Democrats have an opportunity to do the opposite: to use this victory to strengthen our elections rather than tear them down. They should seize this moment to learn from Trump’s attacks on our elections and our democracy.That starts with laying out a more ambitious agenda to limit the ability of Trump, or any president, to threaten an election the way he threatened this one.It also requires accelerating the growth of a new pro-democracy media ecosystem to match the one the right wing has spent years building.Democracy Docket is part of that effort, and it depends on readers like you.In the days ahead, I will have more to say about how I can best serve this growing movement. For now, I’m going back to work.

item.title: Modern Mandolin Quartet
item.author: Flow State
item.content:encoded: Today we’re listening to the Modern Mandolin Quartet, a quartet founded in San Francisco in 1985. Mandonlist Mike Marshall formed it with Dana Rath, John Imholz, and Paul Binkley, with the shared mission of elevating the mandolin as an instrument worthy of classical and contemporary music.Imholz played the larger mandocello and Binkley played the mandola (viola equivalent), mirroring the traditional chamber quartet. Their 2012 record contains a century of American compositions by Copland, Bernstein, Gershwin, and Glass. We’re also playing their 1988 LP, , which plays classical pieces by Bach, Debussy, Ravel, and more.

item.title: The Scope of the Wave
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Just before 2 a.m., I’m trying to make sense of the Senate results. If I’m making sense of this right, Democrats have clearly won 54 senate seats, appear likely to win 55 and could still win 56.The final uncertain seat is in Mississippi. The Times calls it a toss-up with a 61% chance of Republicans winning it. But election watchers I trust seem to think it’s just a bit more likely that Colom will win. To be clear, they’re only talking about likelihoods, and it’s a bit more likely, in their view, that Colom will win. To be fair to the Times, these are models that are fully devised in advance. And this is extremely close. When it’s that down to the wire, it’s down to picayune details, idiosyncrasies of particular counties that may just be hard for a model to fully capture. The people I’m following suggest that in the key counties where votes remain the last ballots tend to lean Democratic.

item.title: Thanks to Everyone Who Joined Our Video-cast
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Thank you to everyone who joined us for tonight’s livecast. We had about a thousand people watching through most of the evening from 8 PM to around 12:30 or so. We really enjoyed it and we hope you did too. We’re going to be doing more of these. As I’ve noted a few times, polling is just a predictive artifact. None of all those polling questions matter now. But one thing is worth observing simply to think clearly about the unpredictability of polling error. It will take a while for numbers folks to crunch all the numbers. But simply look at the Senate races it’s clear that while some polls were accurate quite a number of them significantly underestimated Democratic strength – South Carolina, Texas, Iowa and a number of others. This isn’t an exhaustive list. I’ve been on our video-cast for almost five hours. I’m a bit fried. But again, polling error doesn’t just underestimate Republicans. It goes both ways. It’s unpredictable.

item.title: Humpday Hottie: Paige Spiranac
item.author: Schill
item.content:encoded: Paige Spiranac is an American former professional golfer, social media personality, and sports media figure who became one of the most recognizable personalities in golf. Born in Wheat Ridge, Colorado, in 1993, she grew up in an athletic family and initially pursued gymnastics before focusing on golf.Spiranac played college golf at the University of Arizona and San Diego State University, where she competed at the collegiate level. She later played professionally on developmental golf tours, including the Cactus Tour, where she recorded a victory in 2016. Although her professional playing career was relatively brief, her visibility outside traditional tournament golf grew rapidly.Spiranac became particularly well known through social media, where she combined golf instruction, entertainment, and commentary. Her videos and posts attracted a huge audience, making her one of the most-followed golf personalities online. Her approach was different from traditional golf media, emphasizing accessibility and entertainment alongside the sport itself.She has also worked as a golf commentator, podcast host, and content creator. Her media career has included interviews with professional golfers, instructional material, equipment discussions, and coverage of major golf events.One of the defining aspects of Spiranac’s career has been her role in discussions about how golf is presented to younger and more casual audiences. She has frequently used humor and an informal presentation style rather than the more traditional tone associated with golf broadcasting.Spiranac has also spoken publicly about the criticism and online attention that accompanied her rise to prominence, particularly the way female athletes and sports personalities are treated on social media.Whether discussing golf technique, professional tournaments, equipment, or the culture surrounding the sport, Spiranac has built a career that extends well beyond competitive golf. Her transition from collegiate and professional golfer to a major digital media personality illustrates how social media has changed the traditional boundaries of sports celebrity.

item.title: datasette-apps 0.3a0
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Datasette Apps adds support for hosting and editing custom HTML applications inside of Datasette.These can be created by hand, but it's easier to create them using LLMs via Datasette Agent. This release improves that integration:Apps can now be tagged in Datasette Agent chat messages by typing , which autocompletes from the apps the user has permission to view.New and app_remove_stored_queries() tools let the agent manage which stored queries an app is allowed to call. Granting a write query requires approval from the user first. now checks that each requested stored query exists and that the user can view it, and asks the user to approve any write queries before the app is created.The "View app" buttons shown by the agent tools, and the links on app references, now open the app full screen in the Datasette Agent panel.

item.title: Let’s Do This, People
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: : Okay, we still only have a few states reporting. But there are some important ones. And this is looking like it’s going to be a very long night for Republicans and perhaps not that long a night for reporting results. I don’t want to get ahead of ourselves but the details are looking that way. Buckle up. : If you’re watching individual races don’t put much stock in any results unless you have a good handle on what’s early vote and what’s election day vote. We know that the early vote was landslide margins for Dems. And they’re often counted first. This is why you start to be able to understand what’s happening when you start seeing total results even in small counties. Then you get a real sense of swings. : We’re about to get a bunch of results. But one thing to keep in mind is that we might see a somewhat different story in battlegrounds and non-battleground states. The general take about 2024 was that even though Harris lost, her campaign pushed the battleground further in her direction than the locked down parts of the country. So another possible dynamic to keep in mind. It might be rougher for the GOP outside the battlegrounds. But that can play out in unpredictable ways. You can have a big Dem swing. But in a very Red state most Republicans might still hold on. : Another thing to keep an eye on is when races in what should be safe Republican seats don’t get called right when polls close. They’ll probably win most of those. But you get a read of what’s happening just by when some of these races can’t be called right away even if the Republican likely will end up winning it. : As noted below, join us at 8 PM for our live videocast. For now, we only have reporting from a couple states. But we’re seeing some Republicans in pretty Red districts with real races on their hands. They may win those. But those seats being in contention point toward something bigger than your average wave. We’re seeing substantial swings in Indiana. Keep an eye on Indiana 5, Victoria Spartz’s district. That’s a R+8 Cook PVI district. Trump won it by 17 points in 2024. And she may have a race on her hands. (Remember that midterms can be weird. Different states can have different dynamics.)
