item.title: How Human Civilization Began
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: In a recent video, Kurzgesagt explores what we know about the first human civilizations that formed some 12,000 years ago and how they led to the first cities and the invention of writing.What we know about human history is only a fraction of the full story. Much of the rest is like dark matter, invisible to us. We can’t see it, and we can only see the effects of its presence. But thanks to new techniques for DNA sequencing, dating ancient detritus, mathematical models, and aerial and lidar archaeology, we are now able to get a faint idea of what this world might have looked and felt like.One thing I really appreciate about Kurzgesagt is how each of their videos is accompanied by an extensive list of sources. For instance, I’m not sure I’d heard about the massive Lake Agassiz draining into the world’s oceans and disrupting the entire planet’s climate some 8200 years ago — and there are several primary sources listed for further reading. Here’s how Kurzgesagt tells it:Around the year 3800 of the human era a sudden catastrophe happened in North America. The receding glaciers of the last ice age had created one of the largest lakes in Earth’s history, larger than the Caspian Sea today. It was held back by super massive ice sheets, which formed a gigantic dam. Surprising no one, the dam melted and suddenly failed – the whole lake suddenly drained into the ocean. Global sea levels rose by 1-2 meters and the great conveyor belt that carried warm water northwards slowed down. Across the North Atlantic and Europe, and into the Near East, the climate turned colder and drier – in some regions by several degrees. Rain patterns shifted, summers grew longer and harsher, and a drought lasting well over a century parched the land.We know that during this time all over the world migration towards rivers and lakes sped up — bringing agriculture and technology with them. Some of the most consequential journeys led into the Nile Valley, where farming villages took root and slowly laid the ground for the rich civilization that would one day rise there.Lake Agassiz’s major drainage reorganization events were of such magnitudes that they significantly impacted climate, sea level, and possibly early human civilization. The lake’s enormous freshwater release into the Arctic Ocean has been postulated to have disrupted oceanic circulation and caused temporary cooling. The draining of 13,000 years ago may be the cause of the Younger Dryas stadial. Although disputed, the draining at 9,900–10,000 years ago may be the cause of the 8,200 yr climate event. A study by Turney and Brown links the 8,500-years-ago drainage to the expansion of agriculture from east to west across Europe; they suggest that this drainage may also account for various flood myths of ancient cultures, including the Biblical flood narrative.

item.title: The Timeout Bozo Is Gone
item.author: Samer Kalaf
item.content:encoded: The New York Liberty have decided to get rid of head coach Chris DeMarco after one season, as first reported Tuesday by ESPN. It may come as a surprise to some, since the eighth-seeded Liberty swept the top-seeded Minnesota Lynx in the first round of this year's WNBA playoffs. Looking at the bigger picture, however, this firing was deserved.After that historic playoff upset, the Liberty hit their heads on the ceiling in the semifinal round against the Atlanta Dream. New York was swept in three games, but Game 2 ended in controversy because DeMarco did not use his team's reset timeout to set up a good look at a potential game-tying shot. Instead, Breanna Stewart settled for a heave, and her team lost in overtime, 101-98.After the defeat, both Stewart and DeMarco said the officiating crew incorrectly told them that the Liberty had no timeouts remaining. (Stewart handled most of the explanation, with DeMarco weighing in toward the end.) The WNBA eventually admitted that the refs screwed up, in the most passively worded statement—"a misunderstanding amongst the various parties"—but the league did nothing further to remedy the situation. It merely shifted Fatou Cissoko-Stephens and Kevin Fahy, the two officials in question, to Game 3 of the Valkyries-Aces series, which ended in a less controversial sweep by Golden State. Although the refs deserve the blame there, DeMarco still should have had a coaching staff member assigned to keep track of the timeouts so that he could at least assertively advocate for his own team.

item.title: MAGA panics as post-midterm investigation season looms
item.content:encoded: Among all the gruesome details of allegations both old and new of rape and sexual abuse, there’s one four-word phrase in the new congressional report on Jeffrey Epstein that says a lot about why Donald Trump seems especially unhinged these days: “No statute of limitations.” Led by Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee released their findings on the president’s long and close relationship with the deceased sex offender. The report, citing testimony from 11 women, “indicates that Trump abused, assaulted, and even raped numerous women alongside, and in coordination with, the most infamous sex trafficker in history.”The media response to the allegations was muted, despite compelling new evidence about the extent of Epstein’s sex trafficking ring, suggesting more powerful men were involved than have faced legal repercussions. Perhaps the report was overshadowed by the midterm elections. Or maybe there’s a sense this is “old news” and won’t move the needle. But if Raskin has his way, we’ll all look back to this release as the opening chapter in a season of accountability not just for Trump, but also for various administration figures and MAGA cronies who have enjoyed the legal shield of a Republican congressional majority.Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, they’ll have access to a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players.Democrats are expected to win control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, in the midterm elections. If they do, Raskin and investigators will have a lot more power to investigate not just Trump and the White House, but also various Republican donors, right-wing business interests and other MAGA-aligned power players who have been taking full advantage of the atmosphere of corruption the president has created. The Epstein report is likely just the beginning. As the Washington Post noted on Monday, Democrats “are laying the groundwork for an array of inquiries into President Donald Trump, his family and his administration.” Various business and political leaders are meeting with their lawyers, worried about what Democrats could uncover with this new power. “I haven’t seen this much investigative activity in anticipation of a change in control of a house of Congress ever,” Michael Bopp, who runs a congressional investigations division for the law firm Gibson Dunn, told the Post. There are plenty of signs that it’s dawning on people around Trump that he will be out of office in two short years and that, as the latest Epstein report indicates, the statute of limitations has not run out on many possible crimes committed under the White House’s protection. A recent Zeteo profile of Stephen Miller showed that the White House deputy chief of staff is worried about going to prison if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028. Congressional Democrats keep talking about impeaching Pete Hegseth, and the defense secretary is clearly anxious, reportedly making calls and begging Sen. Marsha Blackburn to appoint him to her Senate seat if, as expected, she wins the Tennessee governor’s race this week. Having a Senate seat would not only prevent impeachment; it could make prosecuting him for alleged war crimes much harder as well. In October Elissa Slotkin of Michigan set off a massive panic on the right when she suggested that there should be a focus on “signature cases” against “people who enabled” Trump. The Michigan senator wanted a “deterrence message” for anyone considering working for Trump, letting them know that committing crimes or otherwise assisting in illegal or corrupt activity might result in “a ton of problems” for them that aren’t worth the risk of legal liability. Fox News and other outlets tried to spin this as Slotkin threatening the mass arrest of young staffers, but the hysteria belies their real worry: Democrats might be able to compile enough evidence that prison is a real threat for many of the people working for Trump. Slotkin’s remarks clearly rattled the White House. Since then, Trump has repeatedly put out word that his underlings should not have to worry about obeying the law because mass pardons are on their way. A few days after Slotkin’s warning, sources inside the White House told the Washington Sun that administration lawyers are looking at “blanket pardons for all employees involved in particular policy areas, such as deportations, war or trade.” Still, the White House is facing serious staffing issues. A September report from the Partnership for Public Service found that people Trump hires quickly leave. Not only have there been a record number of resignations, nearly half of the quitters worked less than a year for Trump. On Monday, Trump himself also told the New York Post that widespread pardons are on the table, not just for his staff, but for allies like Tesla CEO Elon Musk. Musk has good reason to be worried. His brief tenure running DOGE has raised a whole host of questions about what laws were broken by him or by staff carrying out his orders. He’s also under suspicion of messing with Ukraine’s Starlink access, crippling its defenses against the invading Russian military. This may explain why Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars — more than any single donor in history — trying to tilt the elections in the GOP’s favor. Trump and his family members should also be sweating. Trump has often interpreted the Supreme Court’s grant of presidential immunity as all-encompassing, but as Raskin told the New Yorker, he doesn’t see it that way at all. He outlined how the president has made billions in office, roughly $1 million a hour, and that there’s a great deal to learn about where that money is coming from. The Supreme Court’s decision technically only covers crimes committed during the commission of official presidential duties. By definition, Trump’s external money-making enterprises aren’t that. His children are deeply involved in the family business as well. And as the Epstein report made sure to note, some of the crimes Trump and his associates have been accused of committing with his old friend Epstein carry no statute of limitations.It’s tempting to wave all this off as inconsequential, because Trump and his cronies were able to escape severe ramifications the last time around. But to dismiss this talk would be a mistake, in no small part because Democrats need their feet held to the fire. The corruption this time around is far worse than it was in Trump’s first term, more flagrant as the air of lawlessness led to a level of carelessness that creates more prosecutable evidence. The next Democrat in office may not be like Joe Biden, who shied away from aggressive prosecution of Trump and his allies. Some of the politicians whose names are being bandied around — like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — have been highly focused weeding out MAGA corruption. Then there’s the matter of political will. Before now, it was hard to drum up sufficient political support for accountability because voters simply didn’t care enough about corruption. But as the New York Times reported last week, the issue is a rising source concern for voters. Democrats, for one thing, are doing a better job of linking Trump’s self-dealing to the economic problems of ordinary people. For another, the Epstein scandal has broken into national consciousness, and even Republicans are struggling to sufficiently explain why Trump, despite signing a bill to release all Justice Department files related to the case, is refusing to do so.With these winds at their back, Democrats have a much better chance of being able to conduct thorough investigations — and pursue criminal consequences for those found to have broken the law.

item.title: Critical Support To The Shotputting Free Throw Shooter
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: They say that shooting a basketball starts in the legs, especially in the case of free throws. You bend your knees and use the greater, more controlled power source of your legs to generate the force of a shot, only finishing the motion off with a flick of the wrist. That's the theory, anyway. South Florida big Kendall Puryear shoots forth in defiance of that orthodoxy. Puryear shot and missed two free throws in her USF debut on Monday night, though "shot" and "missed" are insufficiently descriptive verbs for whatever the hell is going on here.You'd never teach anything Puryear's doing here: the way she brings her shooting motion to a full halt at the top of her rise, the way she cocks back the ball in one hand as if quivering an arrow, the way she hucks it in a soaring arc as if it's a projectile weapon. One potential explanation for Puryear's form is that she was a champion shot putter throughout high school, winning plentiful district and sectional titles in Missouri. Being good at shot put isn't the sort of thing that necessarily breaks one's form like this, but it feels like a start. She shot 58.1 percent from the line through her first two seasons at Purdue, which isn't great but isn't game-killingly terrible.

item.title: 10 Years of Kottke.org Membership
item.author: Jason Kottke
item.content:encoded: An important KDO milestone whooshed by the other day and I was so heads-down on tuning up the new search engine (more on that below) that I missed it. So: it’s been 10 years since I started the KDO membership program (Quick recap of the value proposition from the membership page FAQ: “kottke.org is my full-time job and member support keeps the site free, open, and available to everyone on an internet that is increasingly paywalled.”)10 years! It is impossible for me to overstate the impact membership has had on my work. Beyond the simple fact that KDO wouldn’t exist without it, membership support allows me the freedom to choose when, where, how, and to work, resulting, IMO, a better place for all of us to spend time.The last couple of years have felt especially membership-inflected and influenced. We’ve been working together on building the KDO comments into a quieter haven for sharing stories and information, outside the social media networks driven by algorithms and outrage. It’s taken time, but KDO is starting to feel like a neighborhood joint where folks can stop by and find a welcoming place for interesting conversation. And more to come!I’ve also been working hard on different ways of helping people find stuff to read/watch/listen to online and just generally making things easier to use around here. There’s:Prometheus, a search & discovery tool for gift links, open only to members for now.KDO site search. Still only open to just members. I spent a lot of time over the past weekend tuning it to return better results, and I think we’re getting somewhere. Improved the speed as well, at the expense of, well, increased expense. It’s still not magic, but I’m hoping to open this up to everyone soon.Underscore, a web-based music player I built for listening to music across multiple streaming platforms while I work. Anyone can listen to my collection and members can compile their own collection to listen to.And this is in addition to the site’s usual service of curated links and posts. A lot of this has happened in just the last month — Jesus, Kottke, slow down! — but I’ve been working on some of these things, on and off, for years. I couldn’t focus on this stuff for months and months earlier this year — launching requires a level of attention that’s difficult for me to muster when other things are going on. Getting the move behind me and establishing myself in surroundings more suitable to my temperament has been a real boon.I hope all of this adds up to a place and project that people want to make use of and support. Twenty-something years into doing KDO as my full-time job, I can honestly say I am enjoying it more than ever. Thanks so much for reading and for your support. If you’re not yet a member and want to join us on this ride, you can check out your membership options here — it only takes a minute to sign up (less if you use Apple Pay or Stripe’s Link autofill).

item.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this .The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other modelsThe prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \ -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-proBut how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \ llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \ -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally".The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample:What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

item.title: Alison Knowles Made Art That Was Designed To Delight And Disappear
item.author: Dan Kois
item.content:encoded: The artist in the video is elfin, mischievous. Even at nearly 80, she is taller than many of the assistants who join her, chopping lettuce at a long counter. Her index finger is bandaged, perhaps from an earlier chopping incident. In the video it is a cold, wet day in 2012 on New York City’s High Line, and Alison Knowles cheerfully narrates the question she assumes passers-by are posing as they walk past this remounting of her most famous work. “You’re making a salad outdoors and in the rain?” she asks. Then she answers: “This must be an art event!”That a theoretical passer-by might reasonably leap to that conclusion—that a half-dozen cooks preparing a tarp-sized salad in a public park is an “art event”—is in no small part thanks to Knowles, who in her six decade-plus career did as much as anyone to expand the boundaries of artistic work. Likely no retrospective could fully capture her capacious artistic practice, but , a retrospective show open at the Grey Art Museum at New York University, serves as an invigorating introduction to a creative force whose questing imagination seems, a year after her death at 92, both sui generis and like a blueprint for the future.Alison Knowles was born in 1933 in Scarsdale, New York. She studied painting at the Pratt Institute, where her father was an administrator, and was on her way to being, in her words, “the next Helen Frankenthaler” when she took a summer course with Josef Albers at Syracuse. Exiled to the basement of the building because of her refusal to follow Albers’ strict instructions, Knowles vowed to stop pursuing “the traditional methods of artmaking,” as she later told an interviewer. One of her early paintings, "Taxis and Busses" (1959-60), hangs near the entrance to the retrospective; it’s a lively mix of oil-painted circus designs and screen-printed commercial logos. It’s one of only two early Knowles paintings that survive; she burned all the others on the beach just a few years later.

item.title: Election 2026 — let’s fucking do this
item.author: Jeff Tiedrich
item.source: everyone is entitled to my own opinion
item.content:encoded: Hey, everyone — today’s election day.I feel good about our chances.Now, of course, I say that while still bearing residual PTSD from telling everyone in 2024 about how good I felt about our chances then. But, nonetheless, today I feel good. Our candidates are young, smart, energetic, charismatic and inspiring. Our side is caring, with a sense of fairness and justice for everyone.Their side sucks all ass.Now, I hear you asking, ‘Uncle Jeff, why are you showing us a photo of just the Pool? I thought you said there was a rally going on.’Silly rabbit, look closer. That the rally. Keep looking, I promise you there’s a rally in there. Come on, zoom way in. : Oh my dear sweet lord, Yup, that’s the rally. The one that was supposed to sum up the entire campaign.Who thought this would be a good idea? Who let Donny do this? Who allowed Dear Leader to go out and humiliate himself like this in public?The answer is ‘no one.’ This all is Donny’s own doing. He picked the location. He chose the subject matter. He’s the one who decided a whole rally should be themed around the Reflecting Pool that wasn’t broken, but nonetheless got the fixed out of it. He’s the one who then didn’t bother to publicize it, or invite voters to attend.Donny’s too demented to understand that stunts like this are completely sabotaging his own party’s chances in the midterms. He thinks he’s fucking crushing it. And no one can stop him.“We were losing on average, TO DEATH, 3— people— a week. And now we don’t have that. We don’t have that.”Excuse me, what even is that gibberish? ‘We were losing on an average to death’? What kind of grammar is that?We were, now? Were there indeed three people getting in a pool that’s 18 to 30 inches deep? That’s quite a statistic. What’s our takeaway, that only Dear Leader can prevent the heartbreak of getting drownalyzed in a thimble full of water?How fucking demented to you have to be to fancy yourself the Un-Drowner of Lost Souls?Republicans should be thanking their lucky stars that the campaign ended yesterday, because we were only two or three more days away from Donny emptying his diaper onto his head and demanding everyone sing along with him to a rousing chorus of Oh, and Republicans? Get ready to bear the brunt of the blame when you lose today. Don’t expect any introspection from Dear Leader. He’s already denying having anything do with loss.“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms. But we gave this a very strong shot.”Got that? If you lose today, Dear Leader had nothing to do with it. It’s a just a thing that happens a sitting president. Poor Donny, bad things always happens him. For sure, reasons abound during every election, as to why one side loses. But in this case, there’s one reason, and one specific reason alone: because everything is fucked to hell, and Dear Leader fucked it.And that’s why that Reflecting Pool really the perfect metaphor for Donny’s entire second term — just not in the way that Donny imagines it is.The entire world is now as fucked to hell as that Pool. Our economy. our healthcare, our immigration, our relationships with both our allies and adversaries, our energy policy, our military readiness, our supply chains, our trade. None of that was broken, but that didn’t stop Preznit Fuckwit from fixing the shit out of it. So here were are, on the morning of the most important election of our lifetimes — just like the last one before it, and the last one before that. It’s exhausting, but that’s how shitty timelines roll. We don’t have the luxury of sitting any of this out.Let’s do this. I like our chances. Let’s put some good people into power, and they can actually fix this shit, the way it’s supposed to be fixed. Let’s have accountability and justice in this country. Let’s stop allowing a greedy criminal to get away with doing whatever the fuck he wants. The same goes for his felonious family and corrupt cronies.We’ve got this, as long as we show up to vote. That’s the easy part. It’s what comes next that’s going to try our souls.Absolutely, there is going to be attempted fuckery. That’s what Donny does when he can’t get his way. He cheats like a whiny little piss-baby.It’s going to get ugly — but so far, judges, lawyers, courts and even Supreme Court Justices have been keeping the 2026 midterms from descending into lawless chaos. I have every reason so expect these bulwarks against anarchy to continue to do so.And on that note, I’m going to give the final word to Joyce Vance today. She’s already said it so well in her post from last night, so there’s no need for me to I reinvent the wheel.If you’re nervous, you’re not alone. Be kind today. Hold a friend’s hand. Donate to a food bank. Get ready to vote and be prepared for the unexpected over the next few days. Remember that giants walk among us: lawyers, activists, pro-democracy politicians, federal judges who believe in the rule of law no matter who appointed them, and ordinary Americans who will be staffing and monitoring the polls to ensure we can all vote and our votes are counted. So be brave. Have courage. Vote.As Joyce says at the end of every one of her posts, we are are in this together.How would some Daily Claudia be right about now?In honor of the day, let’s have Ms Spouse voting absentee on November 2, 2024, from the physical rehab center where she’d been recovering after falling and breaking her hip a few weeks prior.Let’s move on to five months later, Ms Spouse having completely recovered. Here she is, waiting for our rental car at the San Diego Airport Sheridan, on March 16, 2025. That’s right, she made me travel all the way across the country Now let’s turn the camera around, and let Ms Spouse take a photo of me.Have a great Election Day, everyone.here’s your daily reminder that I can be found on Blue Sky at this link.this is going to be my closing message for the foreseeable future: do what you need to do to keep sane. if that means you need to disengage with my daily posts for a while, I get it. this community of ours will still be here when you return.to all the people who have signed on in the days since the election, . settle in as we all try to deal with the shitfuckery that’s ahead of us.we are all in this together, and we are all here for each other.

item.title: America Votes: 'CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA'
item.author: Jason Koebler
item.content:encoded: Happy election day, America. And happy (?) America’s election day, rest of the world. Hope we don’t disappoint you. We heard you like slop so we put slop in your election. That's not quite the right meme, but whatever. You’re going to see lots of politics news today, so let’s get things started here with something completely different: The neverending saga of Ao3’s unexpected downtime and what it’s doing to the fan fiction community. Sam has the scoop:A vibe-coded site that scraped Archive of Our Own (AO3) fanfiction works, reuploaded them and charged for audiobook versions is down now after the creator said they received over 2,000 takedown requests from authors in the single day it was up.ao3.life, a website that sprung up following last week’s announced weeks-long outage of fanfiction repository AO3, scraped the internet for works to populate the site using “a swarm of AI Agents controlling 40 virtual machines were scraping the internet for all drives, scrapes, and sources,” the site’s creator, named Ganesh, wrote on a page apologizing for the entire project. AO3.life went down on Monday evening following widespread backlash from readers and authors on social media. Before it went down, the ao3.life homepage said, “AO3, saved before it slips away. Search every fandom, ship and trope. Read it here, keep the EPUB, or let it read to you when your eyes get tired.” AO3 went down on Thursday following a security incident, according to the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) which owns the repository. The site is expected to be down for as long as four weeks. OTW says no data has been lost. Readers and authors are generally distraught, unable to access the site at all for potentially a month. AO3 hosts nearly 18.5 million works.ao3.life offered works as EPUBs for reading on e-readers, and as AI-generated audiobooks that Ganesh charged for after the first three minutes. They claimed on a page titled “Authors get paid here” that authors would get 91% of the profits, with AO3.life getting 9% to cover “narration and processing” costs. “Your earnings wait for you. You don't need an account here to earn. We hold your share indefinitely until you collect it, however long that takes,” the site said. On AO3, authors can “archive lock” their works, making them visible only to logged-in users, which keeps AI bots like this one from scraping them and also gives better control over how far a work spreads or whether it breaks the containment of the repository’s intended audience. Of course, authors couldn’t access AO3 while it was down to lock their works if they were publicly available before the outage.But some authors reported the archive lock not mattering. “I had everything archive locked on ao3 and it's still all here and I as the author have 0 control over any of my fics on there,” one AO3 author .ao3.life said at the bottom of the homepage that authors could request their works be removed from the site: ”Every work belongs to its author; if one is yours and you want it gone, email legal@ao3.life and it goes.” Proving that you’re the author of the work to ao3.life required authors “leave a note on your AO3 profile so we can confirm it's you,” the site said. But how authors could do that while AO3 was — and still is — completely down is a mystery. Everything has slopified, including our precious “I Voted” stickers. Matthew Gault writes about his disappointment in participating in democracy and receiving this: “It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop ‘I Voted’ sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI. My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. ‘I Voted’ is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: ‘250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY’ and ‘SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.’ Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — ‘CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.’ I assume this was meant to say ‘CELEBRATING FREEDOM,’ but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost.”World of Warcraft Forever is already overrun with AI slop add-ons, according to Joseph and also Sildri Silentcrest, who runs a site called Warcraft Logs. “Two years ago, say we had 200 developers using our API and two or three or four were being abusive. Today, 10,000 developers are using our API and 1,000 are being abusive. The ratio has changed, and that really feels bad.”You know this already, but it’s election day in the United States. Get out there and vote. Stuff I have my eye on today, besides general control of Congress-related questions, mostly have to do with assessing how mad people are about AI, data centers, big tech, and Flock. It will probably take a bit for this to shake out and to understand exactly what happened in the election, but I assume the anti-data center vote is going to be a big one and will come into play in both congressional and Senate races (especially in Michigan and Ohio). I’ve been saying for ages that local elections and local politics matter very much, so I’m curious if any pro-Flock mayors / councilmembers get kicked to the curb, and if any anti-surveillance candidates replace them. If this happens in your town, please let me know by responding to this or shooting me a message on Signal (@jason.404). In California, I’m wondering if the billionaire wealth tax ballot measure will pass, and what the fallout from that will be. Huge lobbying spending by, well, the billionaires, seems to have had a major impact on the polling for that issue. Flock execs Rahul Sidhu (chief strategy officer) and Josh Thomas (head of communications and chief corporate affairs officer) have left the company. Outside of CEO Garrett Langley, Thomas and Sidhu were the two most visible executives at Flock. Sidhu regularly beefed with just about anyone who disagreed with what Flock was doing on X and was one of the more unlikeable internet presences I’ve ever had the pleasure of following, while Thomas largely dealt with journalists and said several extremely wild things in interviews, including “Americans who don’t want their vehicles captured by the company’s surveillance cameras can opt out of society.” Sidhu has gone to work at a16z, which is Flock’s biggest investor. Thomas updated his LinkedIn to read “Fmr Flock Exec.”Little update on yesterday’s blurb about AI slop games being spammed to Itch.io: The platform says it “just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop.” I randomly became aware of a little indie game coded in the early 2000s called “ROM CHECK FAIL” and have spent part of my morning playing it. The game takes various arcade classics like Mario, Space Invaders, Gauntlet, PacMan, etc and randomly switches the characters and enemies every few seconds. This probably doesn’t make much sense, it’s better to just watch or play it. Cops resign after being tracked: The entire police force of Milner, Georgia has resigned after the mayor of the city admits he put a GPS tracker on the police chief’s truck because he was concerned about cops there possibly lying on timesheets. Funny how the police don’t like being surveilled. Thanks for reading 404 Media. In other news, I have finally seen It is possibly too late to do a take on it but you'll probably get one from me eventually anyway. Now go vote!

item.title: Spiders Sleep, But Do They Dream?
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: Jumping spiders in the genus are sometimes called "eight-legged cats" for their large, almost feline eyes. Just like a cat, spiders rely on their eyes to find, track, stalk, chase, and jump on their prey. While other spiders trap food in their webs, spiders hunt insects and even other spiders and their eggs. (The spiders' unusual intelligence inspired Adrian Tchaikovsky's novel , in which spiders evolve and develop civilization on another planet.) So perhaps it is unsurprising that when fringed jumping spiders, or , take time to rest, they resemble cats, too. The spiders, whose bodies are around the size of Cheerios, first search for a safe spot. Then they spin a silken hammock, and groom themselves, cleaning every leg. Then they settle, become motionless, and droop. Their legs curl and occasionally twitch. And they even have little eye movements.Now a group of scientists has proven that these spiders do not just rest, but actually fall asleep. The spiders even experience a stage of sleep characterized by rapid eye movement, or REM, which is the stage of sleep in which we have our most vivid dreams. Their research was recently published in .Tell me this does not look like a cat!
