Article continues below this adMore and more people arrived, until the line crossed Stockton Street, where it then made a left and continued out of view. A B&C staffer came out to greet the line and, more urgent, to politely ask us to adhere to a 10-item ordering limit, with no more than three of any one item. No one objected, because no one wanted to get kicked out of the line and miss out on any of the goodies. I know I didn’t, which was why I stayed firmly anchored in my little spot for an hour and change. B&C had yet to post its daily menu to its Insta page, so I wasn’t sure what I’d be able to order, much less know what I’d want. When workers finally posted a paper menu outside the front door, the woman in front of me in line kindly guarded my spot so that I could go eyeball my choices. Article continues below this adThis was not an easy menu to parse. B&C’s selection relies on you, the customer, to already know the definition of words and phrases like “frangipane,” “diplomat cream” and “eggplant.” Keep in mind that I hadn’t had breakfast yet, so I had to interpret this menu using equal parts coffee and guile. This is the kind of place where orderer’s remorse is a real danger. You think ordering the cronut is the way to go, and then you see someone indulging in a mind-blowing cruffin at the next seat over and realize what you should have gotten, and then you feel like a dummy. That’s a rough moment for any of us. So I became worried that might happen to me this morning. Then, a funny thing happened to ease my angst: The bakery doors opened. When the line started moving and the B&C storefront came into my view, I was treated to the sight of an automated pastry roller flattening out a gigantic slab of French butter. Just butter. The pastry laminating process, on full display. Nothing that came out of that roller could possibly have sucked. I knew I was in good, floured hands. Article continues below this adI made it to the front door and felt like Shackleton after traversing South Georgia Island. The inside of B&C was bright and spacious, with ample waiting room for people who had ordered coffee, plus a shelf of croissant dog toys. The pastries listed on the menu all ranged between five and nine dollars, so I didn’t worry too much about price when making my choices. Instead, I followed my beer gut. A peach cobbler bun topped with creme fraiche and oat crumble? Yes, I’d have that. A “chunky monkey” cruffin, stuffed with like four different things and topped with a different kind of crumble? Better get two of those. A s’mores pain suisse? I didn’t know what a pain suisse was, but the word “s’mores” alone told me I had to have it. Then there was that brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant, which sounded just weird enough to be good. I ordered all of that.Plus a prosciutto and cheese croissant, so that savory items would get at least one representative in the mix. I didn’t have to wait long for my prize box after ordering, and lemme tell you, you get ample-sized pastries for your money at Butter & Crumble. One chunky monkey cruffin would have been enough to feed a birthday party. The outside of it exploded with the salty unctuousness of that steam-rolled butter, but I would hit pay dirt at the cruffin’s center, where I was treated to a bonanza of, deep breath, brown butter chocolate fudge, banana caramel, banana diplomat cream (sounds dirty), and walnut crumble lurking inside. That one was a contender for Best in Box, no doubt.Article continues below this adI sampled more. The ham croissant was tasty, certainly better than the kind available at Burger King, but my sweet tooth demanded something far more evil. So I quickly moved onto the s’mores pain suisse, which was really a s’mores croissant with a crust that was ribbed for her pleasure. As a rule, s’mores-themed desserts are never better than an actual s’more, and such was the case here. The marshmallow fluff, to its credit, is still stuck to my fingers a month later. Then I dug into the peach cobbler bun and the thick squiggle of crème fraiche topping it. This was a good-ass sticky bun, because of course it was. The tag team of brown sugar and butter will always remain undefeated. I could taste that French butter monolith in everything. These were pastries made with great fussiness, but also great love. Butter & Crumble wants to spoil you with indulgence, and everything they serve succeeds in that mission.But it was the last item I sampled that was the truest revelation. This was the brown butter cornmeal twice-baked croissant. I’d saved this one for last, because most everything else I’d ordered bore all of the traditional features I usually look for in a pastry: chocolate, fancified frosting, caramelized goos. The cornmeal croissant was a different animal, and thus took lower priority. This was a traditional croissant filled with (another deep breath) brown butter cornmeal frangipane, caramel and vanilla corn custard; then topped with sweet corn cream and a cornmeal crumble. This was how I learned that a “frangipane” was a kind of almond cream. There is no better way to learn this particular lesson. Article continues below this adBecause not only was the cornmeal pudding croissant — I’ll call it that from here on out for the sake of space — the best item I ordered from Butter & Crumble, it was also one of the best croissants I’ve ever eaten, be it here in America or over in Europe. The cornmeal flavor was much more subtle than the menu description suggested, and the cream and crumble combination on top gave me the same crunch, plus the same “Yay there’s extra frosting!” rush, that I require from any 1,500-calorie breakfast. To my knowledge, no one comes to Butter & Crumble for one specific item on their menu. But if anything from Sophie Smith deserves to go viral among snobs, it’s this one. It’s the corn pudding croissant that needs to step off the foodie runway and break into every chain bakery and grocery store across the country. And I hope that Butter & Crumble helps to make that happen. I’ll remember that croissant, and I hope that, one day, I can take my kids to some nearby, lesser bakery to eat another one. I might even be willing to wait in line.

item.title: I tried the $60 cioppino at San Francisco's oldest restaurant
item.content:encoded: There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.Actually, I didn’t even have to go inside to know I’d be dining somewhere special. The Tadich facade exudes iconography from top to bottom: the classic neon sign hanging overhead, the restaurant’s name splashed in gold lettering across the front window, with the old timey slogan, “The Original Cold Day Restaurant” underneath … even the curtains partially shielding window seat patrons inside from the view of passersby. Standing outside this restaurant, I knew I would be in good hands. Of course I would be.The interior remains equally classic in form. A long, wooden, wraparound bar dominates the center of the dining room, with bolted down stools looming above a herringbone-patterned hardwood floor. Along the walls are sturdy tables covered in white tablecloths and set with no-frills plates and flatware. And the lights are dimmed such that you see everything you want to see and nothing you don’t. This is the kind of place you can walk into at happy hour to feel a little extra grown up. And that’s before you even get the check, which will inevitably take your breath away.Article continues below this adSo what are we eating? Well I hope you like seafood, because that’s what’s on the menu at Tadich. Repeatedly. I sat down with my companions and ruminated over which of roughly 50 ways I could have my Dungeness crab. Would I like it in a salad? In a crabcake? Baked into a casserole? Sauteed in white wine and mushrooms? Much like Swan Oyster Depot, Tadich serves fresh seafood in all of its classic iterations. Only unlike Swan, it has done so since before the Civil War, and with better ambience. For starters, we got an order of raw Miyagi oysters (no relation to the “Karate Kid” character) on the half shell, prawn cocktails, bay shrimp cocktails, a Dungeness crabcake with Old Bay butter, and Dungeness crab salad. We got the crabcake at the behest of our bartender, who insisted that I, being from Maryland, order the West Coast version of my home state’s signature dish. You know, as a little contest.We didn’t have to wait long for our starters to arrive. Tadich Grill is a restaurant for people who do not f—k around, be they seasoned tourists or local tech bigwigs doing a power meal. Suddenly the area of the bar in front of us was covered in more plates than we could fit. I addressed this miniature crisis the only way I knew how: by eating all of the food as quickly as I could. The first Miyagi oyster was all brine before the subsequent ones offered a fuller, creamier texture. The bay shrimp were too small to excite me in any way (same as at Swan; I dunno why you people care about these tiny ass shrimp). The cold prawns were appropriately fresh and meaty, with a suitably biting cocktail sauce for dipping.But all of those were prelude to the crab in its two forms. First the crabcake. Was it as good as a Maryland crabcake? No. That’s not me being territorial. I have had elite crab on the West Coast, and have always been willing to give that crab its due. The problem is that Dungeness crab isn’t as meaty as blue crab, the latter of which is what Maryland crabcakes use exclusively. That renders a Dungeness crabcake mushier, unable to yield cleanly to the fork.Article continues below this adThe salad, on the other hand, was another matter. Served in a glass sundae dish, the salad featured a pile of undressed crabmeat topped with a juicy claw nugget and generous dollop of cocktail sauce. This is Dungeness as it’s meant to be served: cold, elegant, light on the tongue. I ate mine in seconds. Once I’d reached the bed of shredded lettuce under all of that crab, I wanted there to be more crab. Good crab will do that to you. I was skeptical that any of the entrees could top this salad. Ah, but one did.That would be the $60 seafood cioppino, laden with clams, mussels, scallops, white fish, more Dungeness, more prawns, and more of the silly little bay shrimp. You order a dish like this for those ingredients yes, but really you’re ordering it for the unctuous broth that harnesses the flavors of those ingredients all into a single, glorious pool for bread dipping. The cioppino came with thick slices of garlic bread, which I immediately tore up and dunked into all of that savory goodness. When the garlic bread was gone, I kept on doing the same thing with bread from the bread basket. For the sake of diversity, we also ordered seafood saute, which tasted like wedding food and wasn’t anywhere near as good. You can also order steaks and chops from Tadich’s revered mesquite wood grill, but I was both too full and too negligent to do so.Article continues below this adBesides, I needed to save room for dessert, which came in the form of bourbon bread pudding. This is the kind of dessert you order knowing full well that you’ll have to walk home after eating it. It arrives at your table in a cube, because that will be the shape of your body upon consuming it. I had no regrets. The pudding was excellent, and made me feel like a rich man. I needed the walk home anyway. On that walk home, I thought about the slogan painted on Tadich’s front window. Tadich Grill was once named “The Original Cold Day Restaurant,” but not for the reasons you might think. Back in 1882, ownership rechristened it after city tax assessor Alexander Bedlam crowed that it would be a cold day if he were to ever lose reelection. He lost, and the restaurant he frequented got the last laugh. I hope it gets to gloat in similar fashion over certain current, mouthy political figures, because it deserves to. The thought of that kept me nice and toasty as I hoofed my way back to my hotel. I’ve had better food in San Francisco, but sometimes you eat meals where the food isn’t necessarily the point. You can go to Tadich just for that crab salad and be pleased, but it’s the full experience of this restaurant that you’re really paying for: the neon sign, the bartop, the servers and bartenders all dressed in kitchen whites and ties. Above all else, you’re paying for the history. Tadich Grill is a place that could only exist here in San Francisco. You can taste it. Article continues below this ad

item.title: Pumpkin Seeds
item.author: Ernie Smith
item.source: Tedium: The Dull Side of the Internet.
item.content:encoded: Some spare ephemera about Halloween, at exactly the time you need it: A couple days after the fact. We got cryptids, celebs, and even an original tune.Hey all, Ernie here with a piece from David Buck! He’s here to talk about the most tedious holiday, depending on how you hold it: Halloween. (It’s so tedious that we wrote about it late.) Hey, everyone! I’m back! Anyhow, my love of Halloween isn’t dead, but it sure does smell funny these days. Over the past few years, we’ve published a few Halloween specials featuring plenty of spooky, Halloween-themed stuff. We even tried out a short video/podcast thingy. Last year, we presented a sequel of sorts. And this year, we’re continuing that tradition with some more Halloween-flavored treats for the spooky season. So grab yourself a Butterfinger, put on your favorite spooky tunes, and get ready for another helping of Pumpkin Spice Pop Culture. — @ Today’s GIF comes from a piece of classic cheese involving the late Tim Curry, one of the best to ever do it. More about that below. a flying, humanoid monster being seen around Point Pleasant, WV. Sightings continued until late 1967. It was probably just migrating birds, but Mothman continued to be part of the public imagination. It’s perhaps just as recognizable as the Jersey Devil, Bigfoot, or Chupacabra in the Great Hall of Cryptids (an imaginary place I just made up, but, hey, it’d be a pretty bitchin’ museum).Cryptids are the cream of the Halloween cropHalloween isn’t complete without monsters. I’ve read about them, played TTRPG’s that feature them, and even drawn a few, like that mushroom bit baba yaga-style house above.A few years ago, I was an avid viewer of Dr. Emily Zarka’s . It’s a show about the monsters of cultures all around the world. She’s covered by the headless horseman (so have we!), King Kong, and cryptids from around the world.Monsters are always a fascinating topic, particularly lycanthropes. But we got to thinking more about local cryptids. That is, cryptids specific to a certain area. You know, like the Jersey Devil. Only they’re not limited to the United States. These cryptids and stories about them have traveled across the world.Cryptids have long been a fascinating subject for us, so we did a little roundup of the four of the most interesting cryptids we came across.My criteria for these was a) I think they’re interesting and b) I can draw them. You’ll see why that’s important in a moment.If your favorite cryptid isn’t here, I apologize. They’re all great. These just happen to be the ones I like the most right now.Grafton Monster: Grafton, WV. Ah, West Virginia, home to the original sightings of Mothman. The state has another cryptid in its history: the Grafton Monster. It’s supposed to be a tall and pale humanoid creature that may or may not be headless. Oh, and it makes a creepy (sometimes described as “unusual” whistle sound.Just like our good buddy Mothman up there, sightings of the Grafton Monster began around 1964. Journalist Robert Cockrell described the monster as roughly 7 to 9 feet tall. He also said it looked kind of like a seal but it had no head. I imagine it looks a little something like my drawing above (it’s not to scale). The east coast seems to be awash in cryptids. Massachusetts has the Dover Demon. This one is pretty odd. In 1977, a creature with glowing orange eyes that was only four feet tall was spotted on a broken stone wall. 17-year old Bill Bartlett drew a sketchOver the next few nights, more sightings were reported. What the kids described sounded like a gray alien right out of Area 51.What they might have actually seen was a baby moose or a snow owl. Either way, it’s a bizarre local cryptid story and has become legendary around that area of Massachusetts.Tommyknocker: Georgetown, Colorado. Did you know that Tommyknockers are a real Colorado cryptid? No, these aren’t Stephen King’s Tommyknockers. Instead, these guys are like Colorado leprechauns.Sometimes, they’re friendly or described as tricksters. But they’re a Colorado legend, right along with the Yeti’s in Vail, those pesky vampires in Lafayette, and that silly little hotel that inspired in Estes Park. The U.S. has its fair share of local cryptids, but you should see some of the ones from around the world. Take the bunyip, for example. This thing is scary. It’s from aboriginal culture, originally, and is said to resemble a hippo. Or a manatee. Or something with an elongated neck.Either way, it’s an incredibly deadly creature lurking in a swamp in the inner part of the continent. According to the its origin might be related to the rare appearances of seals upstream in Australia. I suppose that makes sense, but imagine running into one of these things in the wild.Cryptids often seem to be based on things that really do exist, but the way we imagine or interact with them is what creates the idea of a monster. The human imagination really is a powerful thing, isn’t it?The year I wrote a silly song for Halloween. Back in those days, I wrote silly bluesy folk songs. I still do. But I used to do it . And I had a ton of fun songs. I’ve never managed to get enough energy together to make a full record. Life has been hectic. Lately, I’ve decided I want to return to what I liked most about this industry: playing music and writing about oddball stuff. With that in mind, I wanted to share the journey of a Halloween-adjacent song I wrote over a decade ago and never got around to until now. So I dug this song up from its grave.A brand-new, oddball song for Halloween that never got the chance to liveLast year, we talked about Phish’s famous Halloween shows and a lot of other Halloween-themed music from some of our favorite musicians. This year, my costume is “nerdy guy who’s really into jam bands.” When you look at me, you can just I like Blues Traveler. A lot. (Editor’s note: I also enjoy Blues Traveler … when John Popper is not blocking me on social media.) So, of course, I’ll be talking more about my own foray into “scary melodies”.I’ve been reflecting on something related to my personal musical journey. About a decade ago (perhaps a few years earlier), I wrote what I considered a “Halloween song.” My goal was to make a video for it, release it online, and submit it to .As I’ve written previously, getting airplay on was a singular dream of mine for a long time. It did eventually happen, but not until a few years before Dr. D announced his retirement. It’s been a year since the show ended.So where does that leave my career ambitions? I dunno. I’ve been honing my craft and playing for fun for years. So it doesn’t really affect things much. The weird music pipeline is just a bit different.But I want to talk about that Halloween song I wrote so many years ago. I called it “Beware, the Poltergeist” because I thought it sounded fun and kind of cool. It might have been based on a short story or TV episode, but I just don’t exactly recall where it came from.I started the song, wrote some music, and finished a verse/pre-chorus, but have just never been able to finish or expand it meaningfully. It’s a bluesy tune about a poltergeist who’s kind of a jerk. I thought it was hilarious, and I dig the way I have the melody match the lyric.The song starts like this (it was originally in the key of B):There’s a ghost in my houseTrying to push me down a staircaseThere’s a ghost in my houseThrowing things all over the placeSee? This is just proof that you don’t need an LLM to write a dumb song. I was writing dumb songs before ChatGPT hit the scene. Also, don’t use an LLM to help you be creative. If you didn’t bother to write it yourself, I don’t want to read or listen to it. Hey, look! Some clouds. I’ll be right back.(Incomprehensible ranting and light swearing about outsourcing thinking and creativity in the direction of no one in particular)Okay. I’m back. Anyhow, I wrote a chorus/pre-chorus. It isn’t Vonnegut, but I like it. I’m not sure if I actually it to say much. After that, the song repeats the “there’s a ghost in my house” bit, followed by an off-hand comment about how much he sucks.Obviously, the song isn’t going to make it onto the show now. But that’s not the reason I revisit it every so often. I like it. It’s fun to play. I just never managed to finish it. The other day, however, I realized something: it actually finished, and it always has been. I was just overthinking it and playing it in the wrong tuning.Not everything needs to be edited or rewritten to death. Sometimes, there’s value in a simple song with an extended guitar bit.I never recorded it. Until now. So, this Halloween, I present the second-ever released song by my one-man band (which I’m calling Asthmatic Whales nowadays; it used to be The Nostalgia Ward): “Beware, the Poltergeist.”And there you have it. A silly Halloween song for the truly scary times we’re living in. I hope you enjoyed it as much as I did dusting it off and revisiting it. Thanks for reading, and I hope you have a very Happy Halloween.Those homebrew NES games Spirit Halloween sells? Surprisingly goodIn last year’s NES roundup, I briefly mentioned how Spirit Halloween was selling NES carts containing the homebrew title Haunted: Halloween ‘86: The Curse of Possum Hollow. What I didn’t talk about is just how freaking amazing this game series is. That’s one of three games in the series, alongside , and .These games are standouts among NES homebrew titles; they have a and feel to them. However, the stories are more developed, you can switch characters, there are extra move sets (which is not typical in most NES games), and I had a ton of fun playing through them.So let’s look at the trilogy. I only own the first two games (purchased directly from Itch.Io)I haven’t had the opportunity to play yet, but if it’s anything like the first two (and particularly, like ), I know I’m going to love it.I think the first two are definitely standout titles and I recommend them for some 8-bit Halloween fun. I’ve mentioned or outright talked about show on . Although he’s been officially retired for a year now, I still listen to and collect the show. I haven’t been able to keep up with the community much (although I’d like to) due to life, but I know the fans are still out there. Halloween is a time we “Dementians” loved, so I always think about the show a lot more often around this time of year. I also couldn’t help but think that the good Doctor would have done a nice tribute to the late Tim Curry on his show back in August, if it hadn’t gone off the air. been a rough one, both for the world and in terms of some of our favorite entertainers passing.We lost Tim Curry, Dolly Parton, and Patrick Stewart all within a few months of each other. In honor of these icons, here are a few fun facts about each that relate to Halloween:Tim Curry once recorded a classic cheeseball song for the low-budget ’80s HBO movie called “Halloween Song.” As wrote about it in 2020, “It has remained one of the most wonderful, terrible, bizarre videos of all time, thanks to its unapologetic synthesizer score, baffling lyrics, and the cheapest special effects the ‘80s had to offer—but there’s more to it than its cheesiness. Much more.” (Speaking of Curry, check out this Rocky Horror Picture Showaudience participation recording from 1983.) then rented it to someone without telling his tenants about it. (They figured it out, and then he came clean.) It’s a tale that he wrote about in his book .It’s a sad time, but hopefully, we’ve been able to cheer you up and boost your spirits a bit during this Halloween season (which seems to be shrinking each year, or maybe I’m just getting old). Thanks for reading, and until next time, have a very Happy Halloween!

item.title: llm 0.37
item.author: Simon Willison
item.content:encoded: There's a of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.I added and , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to - half the price of the previous default, .LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video.A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.

item.title: How Ditching Norms and Guardrails Was Trump’s Undoing
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: Two years on from Donald Trump’s 2024 second election to the presidency we can identify clear patterns separating Term One and Term Two. I’ve noted at other times that for all the norm-busting, outrages and crimes of Term One, if you were a regular person who didn’t pay much attention to politics, very little of it intruded into your life. And the economy remained buoyant. The fact that Trump inherited a strong economy doesn’t matter in terms of public tolerance.Of course, Trump still got quite unpopular. But to the extent that the Trump opposition kept up that resigned refrain “Nothing matters” there was a reason: If you simply didn’t pay attention to politics, most people could say, ‘Yeah, he’s weird but how is it affecting me?’ And at least before COVID there was much less — in terms of things that are materially affecting your life today — that many Trump foes allowed.

item.title: Canelo Alvarez Claims Another Belt. Now What?
item.author: Dave McKenna
item.content:encoded: Saul “Canelo” Alvarez won another title over the weekend while making a ton of money and looking damn good in the ring. So why is it so easy to feel sorry for him? The deserving Mexican legend got past a quick start from reigning WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli, then pounded the essentially unknown underdog champ’s will to win out of him and took his belt via unanimous decision on Saturday in front of a disinterested crowd in a small arena in Riyadh. The start of the fight was delayed for about an hour, reportedly because Turki Al-Sheikh, the Saudis’ sweet science point man, couldn’t be bothered to show up on time. When the opening bell finally rang, Mbilli started strong. The undefeated 31-year-old Frenchman, who won his first belt last year with a vicious first-round knockout of Maciej Sulecki, was not only younger, bigger and faster than the grizzled veteran, he was also busier. Mbilli was shoving Canelo into corners and throwing punches in bunches. Canelo was accurate with his counters, but Mbilli was more than holding his own early on. In the third round, when Canelo had his back against the ropes, he began pounding his own chest and inviting Mbilli to take more shots at him. Canelo had made the very same gestures during a 2022 loss to light heavyweight champion Dmitry Bivol, perhaps to fire himself up, but in that case ended up bringing himself more pain.

item.title: Fox News loses its grip on the culture wars
item.content:encoded: In any other election cycle, a viral Fox News gaffe would have registered only as a momentary laugh. Last week, reporter Lucas Tomlinson was covering a South Carolina rally for incumbent Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who is seeking to serve a full term following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. In reality, the event was more about Donald Trump, who had flown to the Palmetto State to help shore up Graham’s candidacy, which increasingly appears to be at-risk. Spotting a middle-aged white man with a beard, Tomlinson assumed he was about to get some choice footage of a gushing Trump superfan. Instead, Tom Hoyle, with an admirable deadpan, joked that he had turned out for the rally because he was too young to have witnessed the 1978 Jonestown massacre, in which 918 followers of Rev. Jim Jones died after drinking a fruit drink laced with poison. “There’s nothing like seeing a cult right up front, man,” he added.“All right, maybe this is not a Trump supporter,” Tomlinson said, scurrying away. The surreal moment capped what has been a desultory midterm election season for Fox, a network that bills itself as “news” but has long been seen by fans and detractors alike as Republican propaganda. Despite their largely worshipful coverage of the president, Trump has been complaining that the network isn’t doing enough to salvage the campaigns of the GOP. “FoxNews is spending far too much time putting on the OPPONENTS of Republican Party Candidates,” he recently posted on Truth Social, echoing his prior complaints that the network focuses too much on the Democrats running this cycle than on their Republican opponents. Trump is not wrong about the coverage tilt. According to Media Matters, during this election cycle the network has mentioned the names of Democratic candidates at over three times the rate of Republicans. That disparity, though, doesn’t mean the coverage is sympathetic. To the contrary: Fox producers likely recognize that this year’s GOP field of candidates is deeply uninspiring. Some, such as Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor of Ohio, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is seeking a Senate seat, are so repulsive that even lifelong Republicans can’t pretend to like them.This season, Democratic candidates are making more compelling TV, particularly the charismatic incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., Michigan’s Senate nominee Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Texas state representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton. The most Fox News can hope for is to hijack these candidates’ ability to command attention, and then use it to drive negative polarization with endless “who do these people think they are?” outrage. But then again, the network knows its audience. As Salon’s Sophia Tesfaye recently noted, it’s not like Fox News knows what else to do. The hosts, she writes, have been grabbing wildly at straws, praying they can find any story to spark culture war hysteria that will distract voters from serious issues like inflation, the war with Iran or the metastasizing deportation crisis. The network tried to make hay out of the French riots, but even Fox viewers struggled to see why student protests in Paris matter to America. It attempted to pretend Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., was calling for mass arrests of young Republicans when she was asked during a recent appearance about holding the GOP accountable, but that never really caught on either. A last-minute gambit to feign outrage over Barack Obama’s recent joke comparing Trump’s White House decor to the Cheesecake Factory fizzled out as well, likely because it simply reminded people of how the current resident is defiling the People’s House. Part of Fox’s problem is immediate. Many voters’ economic woes are sky-high, making it hard for culture war nonsense to feel relevant. But there’s also a longer-term problem for the network, which is that they don’t make as much sense as they used to.Fox News has long existed to dress up gutter bigotries and far-right paranoia in the clothes of respectable news coverage, mostly through the use of dog whistles and innuendo. In the past, winks at some of the fouler ideas out there was enough to titillate the audience while keeping up the pretense of respectability. But now, that stuff seems dated and out of touch. This is an era when, as Jamelle Bouie of New York Times said on YouTube, the actual president offers “Klansman-level racism” from the campaign stump, calling Black people “low IQ,” flinging a slur for transgender people at Democratic politicians and suggesting that El-Sayed’s Muslim faith makes him a terrorist. Right-wing social media, especially the Elon Musk-owned X, reads like Stormfront message boards from the 1990s, with Musk himself regularly promoting white nationalist ideas and memes. Former Fox hosts Megyn Kelly and Tucker Carlson offer their former employer stiff competition by being more dishonest and outrageous than the lawsuit-wary network can be, with segments suggesting only supermodel-hot women get raped or that Holocaust deniers have a point. But according to Salon’s Alex Galbraith, one Fox host seems to be getting sick of his network’s culture war strategy. Jesse Watters has complained openly on air about how bad the GOP is doing and how Fox coverage isn’t doing much to excite their audience. In one particularly telling segment, he lashed out about the relentless attention Fox News gives to non-stories from the WNBA, including hysteria over trans players, of which there are zero.“I don’t want to push this story anymore!” Watters said. “I want to leave this story alone! I am no longer talking about the WNBA. As of now, I boycott this segment.”Although his reasoning may differ, the host is right that the Fox fixation on the WNBA is stupid. The league has become such an obsession on the right because, plainly put, many male conservatives hate seeing female athletes perform feats they couldn’t even manage in their youth. They want to end professional women’s sports and return to the sexist delusion that all men are stronger and faster than all women. This much is evident in how real-life right-wingers behave toward the WNBA, such as going so far as to buy tickets so they can throw sex toys at the players. Fox hosts are careful to never say outright that women shouldn’t play sports; that, as they well know, could alienate millions of Republican voters, especially women and fathers of female athletes who are more moderate on this issue. Instead, the network attempts to hijack the antipathy many conservatives feel toward female basketball players with their traditional wink-and-nudge coverage, pretending they want to “clean up” the sport. This preserves the illusion that the right doesn’t hate female athletes while portraying the players — the white ones at least — as fragile, helping to reassure an insecure male audience. In the past, this kind of tap dance has worked. Now, as Watters implied, it’s floundering, feeling much too tepid when compared Fox’s online competitors and actual politicians flinging unprintable slurs. Watters suggested as much during another segment, when he argued that Republicans need more “fear porn” if they want to win.His use of the word “porn” is telling. Watters was arguing that it doesn’t do to be coy any longer — that only the hard-core stuff will move the base. But for Fox News, that would come at the cost of losing advertising dollars and the eyeballs of less radical viewers. This is a true dilemma — and it’s one that couldn’t happen to a more deserving network.

item.title: Falling Down
item.author: Miss Cellania
item.content:encoded: Josh Johnson is great on The Daily Show, but his stand up routines are treasures. He is 36 years old. That's old enough to give up your youthful pride, but still young enough to not worry about becoming seriously injured from a fall, so it's fair grounds for a few jokes. Me, I'm now at the age that I take great care not to fall at all. My doc asked if I've fallen in the last couple of years, and I told her no, I use handrails religiously and I throw out any slippery shoes or rugs. Then she was concerned about my concern. Do I have a problem with balance? No, but I saw what a fall and a broken hip did to my mother. She understood that well. Oh, I've had a few memorable falls. That time an aluminum ladder bent and failed while I was cleaning out the gutters. The last time I roller bladed and my daughter wanted to call 911 because I took time to assess before getting up. The one that left my left shoulder permanently weak. But those were all years ago.

item.title: How The Golden State Valkyries Won The Most Unlikely Championship
item.author: Patrick Redford
item.content:encoded: Every championship is different, though they're all composed of the same emotional materials. A champion is supposed to have overcome circumstances, smelting the raw materials of loss and pain into a durable alloy of resolve. For fanbases, titles are redemptive, victory transmuting heartbreak into joy. The form can accommodate many particularities, but whatever the preceding heartbreak, a championship's message is always the same: It was all worth it.This template breaks down in the case of the Golden State Valkyries. They haven't had to overcome anything. They've enjoyed ubiquitous, unqualified adoration from the entire region since they flashed into existence two years ago. As I watched the confetti rain down on the freshly crowned WNBA champs and 18,000 screaming fans in San Francisco on Saturday night, I was struck foremost by a sense of surreality. None of this was supposed to happen. Owner Joe Lacob made waves by boasting that the Valks would win a title within five years, only for reality to prove a then-bold prediction needlessly conservative. This championship redeemed no visible struggle; there was no narrative convention to adhere to. So how do you make sense of something this unexpected?I think the place to start is with the fans, the bloc of people who expected it the most. One of the more remarkable early developments of the Valkyries' rise was the immediate coherence of a huge fanbase. You'll see in every writeup that the Valks have sold out every single game of their existence, at an NBA arena no less. That only hints at the broader dynamics that have made this team so beloved since before there were players on a team to even love in the first place. The ongoing women's sports boom started booming away from the Bay Area, leaving people in the region to look enviously over at their counterparts in Los Angeles or Portland and wonder when it would be our turn. The NWSL's Bay FC started playing a year before the Valkyries, though they were all the way down in San Jose, an hour from either San Francisco or Oakland, and therefore have never been as easily integrated into the cultural fabric of the region.

item.title: Michigan Really Dodged A Bullet
item.author: Lauren Theisen
item.content:encoded: Everyone in Detroit has a responsibility to keep Haley Stevens away from the Gordie Howe Bridge today, because at the rate she's going, she'll burn that one, too. An outgoing House rep and failed Democratic candidate for Senate who lost to Abdul El-Sayed in a hotly contested Michigan primary earlier this year, Stevens has made the news cycle in the lead-up to Tuesday's general election all about her. While she initially absorbed her August primary defeat without entering into a gigantic public meltdown, over the past several days she has shuffled, then walked, then full-on sprinted toward Republican candidate Mike Rogers, officially endorsing him to the ire of Dems everywhere. Even Chuck Schumer, who never met a centrist he couldn't make excuses for, called it a "despicable betrayal."What exactly happened to cause Stevens to explode like this? An easy target for blame here is Stevens's delectably named fiance, Jason Turkish, who has gone on a media tour of his own, trying to tie El-Sayed's campaign to antisemitism. But Stevens is 43 years old, so the "it's because of a boy" excuse feels insufficient, and downright rude for depriving her of agency when it comes to detonating her career. A more compelling, though still quite sad, explanation is just that she's a sore loser who thought she was owed a Senate seat, and still can't accept that she didn't get it despite tens of millions of dollars backing her in the primary. In this view, her crash-out is not just malicious—though it definitely is—but also immature.In an Anderson Cooper CNN interview Sunday evening, Stevens seemed like she was thinking through her ideas about 10 seconds after they left her mouth. She somehow attempted to square the idea that she wanted Democrats to win control of the Senate, even while rooting and voting against El-Sayed in a critical election to that whole endeavor. This interview was nothing close to an ambush, and yet Stevens, given repeated chances, couldn't come up with a message that made even a lick of sense. That nasally Michigander accent sure sounds a lot better when I hear it at Culver's than when it's being used to try to sabotage the future of the country.

item.title: The Ravens Have Withered Into Mediocrity
item.author: Israel Daramola
item.content:encoded: It's silly to pretend that some otherworldly deity is determining the fates of your favorite sports teams, but what else am I supposed to believe when Lamar Jackson, who had been sidelined with a vaguely described ankle sprain for three games, finally makes it back on the field against the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, only to immediately jam his thumb and leave after one play on offense? The Baltimore Ravens quarterback is most likely out for the rest of the season, as the injury to his throwing hand will require surgery and a trip to the IR.Watching Jackson leave the game, which the Ravens lost 36-10 after also losing backup QB Tyler Huntley to injury, felt similar to when Aaron Rodgers, fresh from carrying the American flag onto the field as a New York Jet for the first time, was taken out for the season on his first drive. That moment marked the beginning of the end for Rodgers and the Jets, as they never captured the magic they hoped to create (Rodgers went 5-12 as the starter the following season). Will it be the same for Lamar Jackson?I've been a fan of Jackson since 2016, when I watched him completely dismantle my school, Florida State, while he was at Louisville on his way to winning the Heisman. He's been one of the most exciting players in football for the past decade. Today, though, I can't help but return to the feeling I had in January 2025, when I watched Mark Andrews drop a pass for a two-point conversion in the divisional round of the playoffs against the Bills, a play which could've sent the game to overtime. In that moment, I felt in my bones that it was over for this version of the Ravens. Not necessarily for Jackson, who was playing his best ball at that point, but for the rest of the team.

item.title: Brighton Is This Season’s Giant Killer
item.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
item.content:encoded: It's not particularly surprising to look at the top of the table in the Premier League and see Arsenal and Manchester City. Aside from Liverpool's 2024-25 title-winning campaign, those two sides have dominated the last half decade in England's top flight, and though City has a pending punishment that might shoot them down the pyramid, it's safe to say that these are the two best teams in the best league. Arsenal and City have another thing in common, though, besides their lofty spots on the table: They have both been pecked by the Seagulls of Brighton & Hove Albion.If one were to look at the advanced stats from Saturday's match between Manchester City and Brighton, without looking at the score, it would be safe to assume that City ran rampant. Shots, possession, xG, passing accuracy, dribbles—by every metric, City had statistical supremacy at its home ground. Well, every metric but the one that matters: goals scored. Thanks to an 11th-minute Yasin Ayari tally, Brighton came away from Saturday's match with its first-ever win at the Etihad Stadium, the most goals scored in the Premier League, and a stranglehold on third place. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BtDH-zkXi1A

item.title: Kimi Antonelli Conquers The World
item.author: Kathryn Xu
item.content:encoded: This year, Kimi Antonelli got lucky. Antonelli drives the fastest car on the grid. He is young—very recently a teenager, even; he turned 20 in August—and that means when faced with an entirely new and controversial ruleset, he didn't have years of prior programming to overcome. Despite his youth, Antonelli has a good sense of narrative satisfaction. This Sunday, during the Mexican Grand Prix, he made sure to snag a podium place in the race where he became the youngest-ever Formula 1 driver to win a Drivers' Championship, hoisted in celebration by the generational superstars before him. Past, present, future.It was the third iteration of an Antonelli–Max Verstappen–Lewis Hamilton podium this year. When the podium roster first occurred in Canada, still early in the season, it was already tempting to refer to the moment as legendary: Antonelli was riding a four-race win streak, and led his much more experienced teammate, George Russell, by 43 points in the championship. But last year proved that inexperienced winners can lose championships even after being staked to larger, later leads, and Antonelli is as inexperienced as it gets, while Russell was getting unlucky with engine failures and mechanical issues. Antonelli had a substantial slump in form over the summer the previous year as a rookie, after a string of good performances to start the season. Over the same stretch of the calendar this year, Antonelli suffered two engine failures from strong positions and otherwise earned a podium. Put aside those two engine failures, and so far this season, the only other race in which he did not finish on the podium was the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, where he finished P5.Formula 1 is a sport in which it is notoriously difficult to distinguish generational talents by their skill rather than by their results. Even the greatest drivers of all time cannot overcome massive gaps in machinery. Even a generational driver will need the correct team, the correct car, the correct regulations, the correct teammate, the correct timing; a generational driver must deliver several seasons of consistent results to prove their standing. But last year provided a timely example of what it looks like when two merely very good drivers, matched in their very-goodness, are given a rocketship to guide to a championship: a close but not particularly exciting battle marked more by ass-over-heels fumbling and obnoxious team orders than iconic victories.

item.content:encoded: The unofficial "motto" of TYWKIWDBI is "you learn something every day." The phrase is not incorporated into the template title page, but I use it often as a closing statement when posting interesting stuff that's new to me. Earlier this week I encountered somewhere on Facebook the observation that the phrase "I hear, I see, I learn" is properly translated into Latin as "Audio, video, disco." I'm 60+ years away from my last Latin class, but I suspect there are some scholarly readers out there who can confirm or clarify this quite interesting discovery.

item.title: How to Assess the Election Day Risk of Trump’s Lawless Attack on the Midterms
item.author: David Kurtz
item.content:encoded: How to Think About Election Day ThreatsWith the worst of Trump’s pre-election attacks on the midterms either failed or foundering, let’s turn to the next act in this saga: scenarios for election interference on Election Day itself.Trump’s attack on free and fair elections has been persistent but also opportunistic, operating less from a master plan than a series of impulses and lurching efforts. That makes it hard to predict, though some telltale patterns do emerge.While we don’t know what Trump or his DOJ and DHS may have in store for Election Day, it is when his attack could get its most ugly, with particular concerns around state-sanctioned violence. But that’s at one end of the spectrum and there’s a lot of other higher risk but lower impact possibilities for tomorrow.None of this is intended be predictive. I just want to frame up for you what to be looking for and how to think about the Election Days threats. The risks exist along a continuum that includes everything from fairly normal Election Day complications to what might look like a coup.The range of Election Day concerns is so broad that it’s helpful to divide them into two categories: (i) transitory scenarios that bear mostly on Election Day itself; and (ii) scenarios that are likely to carry over into the immediate post-election period, including those intended to set the stage for post-election challenges.It’s not so much that one bucket is more serious than the other (although kinda, as you’ll see below) or that the impacts are more or less real. It’s just that the first bucket of scenarios are mostly one and done on Election Day, and the second bucket of scenarios will persist into the fractious post-election landscape between the polls closing and the state-by-state certifications of their elections.Election Day scenarios that are likely to be short-lived include, in rough order from rare to more common:denying or limiting access to polling places, including disrupting and impeding voting;threatening and intimidating voters and election workers at polling places, vote-counting centers, and the offices of elections officials;misusing law enforcement or federal agents, including ICE, to instill fear and cast a pall over the election;disputes over poll opening and closing times; long lines at polling places; ballot shortages; ballot and voting machine errors and snafus.(The last item above encompasses typically discrete issues that pop up around the country in every national election but which rarely impact election results. They often get widespread and frenzied news coverage in the morning and afternoon of Election Day, when the news is otherwise slow because campaigning is done and all there is to do is wait until the results start to come in.)The defining element of the scenarios in this first bucket is that they largely abate once the polls close. It is common for these concerns to take on outsized significance for a few hours on Election Day and then vanish from the national discourse. But they carry the risk of mushrooming into something bigger, especially this year, such as being used as a pretext to take more dramatic direct action to intervene in the election.One last point: If there is any kind of concerted, pre-planned, extralegal attempt by the Trump administration to use the powers of the federal government to intervene in the election while voting is underway, we might first detect it among the actions listed above. It may start ambiguously as a prelude to the more direct interventions below.Bucket No. 2: The Big UgliesThe second bucket of Election Day scenarios contains the most egregious, over-the-top tools in the authoritarian tool chest. The risk of the worst of these actually coming to pass is the highest it’s been in any of our lifetimes, but it still remains a fairly low risk overall. The impact though would be devastating.The Election Day interference that will persist into the post-election phase includes, in rough order of less likely to more likely:destroying ballots or otherwise compromising election security and integrity, including by foreign actors;direct intervention by law enforcement or federal agents, including ICE, in polling places, vote-counting centers, and the offices of elections officials;detaining, arresting, or charging elections workers and officials;seizing ballots, ballot boxes, voting machines, and tabulating equipment;sequestering whole categories of already-cast ballots;mass challenges of already-cast ballots;widespread challenges of normal Election Day processes and procedures;refusal of individual candidates to concede after clear election defeats;refusal to concede the loss of the House or Senate despite decisive election results;inventing new pretexts and reusing old ones to refuse to accept the results of the election overall.The scenarios in the second bucket range from grossly unlawful to the kinds of election delegitimization and extreme gamesmanship that we’ve seen throughout the Trump era but which aren’t per se illegal. It may be difficult on Election Day itself to identify immediately which election challenges are reasonably legitimate under the law — and which are not. That will shake out in the post-election period, but we may get an initial glimpse of them before Election Day is over.The dividing line between the two buckets of scenarios above is imperfect and in some instances could get pretty blurry pretty fast. The line between federal agents vaguely intimidating voters near polling places versus directly intervening at a polling place versus detaining election workers can be crossed in a cascading series of failures within minutes.The astute reader will also note that late on Election Day, after the polls close, is by definition the post-election period. So things like disrupting the tabulating of the votes or seizing tabulating equipment late tomorrow night might not technically be an Election Day concern. Point taken. But for the purpose of broadly alerting you to what to look out for tomorrow I didn’t want to arbitrarily cut it off when polls close, especially with our time zone differences, which puts different parts of the country in different phases of Election Day.I haven’t really entertained here the worst of the worst fears: that the 2024 election was the last free and fair election or that the military will be deployed. I don’t think those are realistic scenarios.Even the worst of the scenarios I do list above I expect would happen sporadically and in specific jurisdictions where either the election is close or Trump wants to make a point of dominance and punishment. In other words, I think it will likely follow the patterns of the rest of the Trump II presidency.If you’re looking for a gut check, here it is: I don’t expect the worst of the above scenarios to come to pass.U.S. elections are too decentralized and the powers of the executive branch alone are too limited in state-run elections for the nightmare scenarios to be more than a fairly remote risk. But an erratic head of state with authoritarian impulses who has built a cult of personality within the ranks of federal officials, runs a supine Department of Justice directly from the White House, and has an overfunded DHS at his disposal remains a very real risk, especially considering how huge the potential downside is.I am most concerned about extreme Republican gamesmanship pushing the legal and political envelope for months to deny winning Democrats a majority in the House or Senate. Under that scenario, the shenanigans would start on Election Day and persist into January and perhaps beyond.Even the perfectly legal contest of the 2008 Senate election in Minnesota denied Senate Democrats a 60th vote for months until Al Franken was finally seated in July 2009. Think of it as GOP transgression on steroids, drawing on elements of the 2000 Florida recount, , Jan. 6, and the invasive federal immigration operations in blue cities.While I’m most concerned about that scenario — which would be very on brand for Trump II Republicans — I still wouldn’t rate it as likely, largely because Republicans will need lots of plausibly close races to maximize chaos — and polling suggests a blue wave. Decisive Democratic victories are the best way to mitigate this risk — but it shouldn’t take a wave election for the rule of law to prevail. Alas, here we are.For the latest developments on all these fronts and everything else about the election, I’d urge you to monitor TPM’s latest live blog.

item.title: Nikita Kucherov Wants Out, And He’s Not Alone
item.author: Ray Ratto
item.content:encoded: There is a sign outside the NHL league offices in New York and Toronto (yep, there are two of them) stolen from construction sites that reads: "[Number Of] Days Since The Last Trade Demand." The current number is 3, and the latest is the strangest so far.It came from Tampa's notoriously taciturn star Nikita Kucherov, who had told his teammates on a team flight that he 1) would not re-sign with the Lightning next summer, 2) wants to be traded somewhere else, and 3) intends to keep playing for the time being while his wishes are accommodated by the team. That last part won him the defense of his coach, Jon Cooper, but it also won a public rejection from general manager Julien BriseBois. So yeah, stay tuned for more fun in our next exciting episode.Kucherov is the fourth big-name NHL player to seek immediate relocation to the players' new favorite team, SOTH (Somewhere Other Than Here). His pursuit of SOTH has been more amicable than his peers' because he didn't make a public show of his unhappiness (that's what agents are for) and is not refusing to play. Indeed, he assisted on three of the four Tampa Bay goals in Saturday's 5-4 shootout loss to the highly ordinary Predators, so a case can be made that he is still giving his all for the olde towne team. A better case could probably have been made if we had bothered to watch the game, but transparency requires that we admit we were watching the WNBA, because every Game 7 is by definition better than every other game in any other sport at any other time.

item.title: Voting in 2026 Is Getting an AI Slop 'I Voted' Sticker
item.author: Matthew Gault
item.content:encoded: It’s a small pleasure, but receiving an “I Voted” sticker after casting my ballot is one of my favorite parts of the whole voting process. I slap the sticker on my chest and spend the rest of the day feeling like I accomplished a little something. I participated in democracy and everyone who sees me will know it. Artificial intelligence robbed me of that small joy this year and replaced it with a small horror. My “I Voted” sticker is AI-generated slop. Getting a little sticker when you vote has been a tradition in the US . It’s a symbol of the election cycle. People take selfies and post them or share them with friends. It’s a celebration of democracy and a small way to pressure people into going to the ballot box. The voting sticker has been subject to every kind of discourse imaginable. Are “I Voted” stickers worth the cost? Wondered Marketplace in 2020. A cemetery in New York has spent time and money of Susan B Anthony because voters coat it in stickers during voting season. In 2008, companies like Starbucks and Ben and Jerry’s of election laws for offering free treats to people who showed their “I Voted” stickers.It’s appropriate but depressing that I got an AI slop “I Voted” sticker in 2026, the year it feels like the mainstream began to reckon with AI.My sticker is ugly. It’s a busy circular nightmare. “I Voted” is spelled out in small bronze text at the top of the ring. Bronze laurels encircle a bronze bald eagle that stretches atop the American flag. Below this is more text: “250 YEARS ANNIVERSARY” and "SEMIQUENCENTENNIAL.” Below that, another line reads — as best I can tell — “CEKEVPATIVG EDELDOA.” I assume this was meant to say “CELEBRATING FREEDOM," but whoever churned out this slop wasn’t using the latest models and the fine detail is lost.I put the sticker on reluctantly, but I was not proud. I sent a photo of the offending sticker to journalist friends with my face cropped out. They immediately noticed it was AI-generated. I did not post my sticker online. I shared it with no one else. My democratic joy turned to shame.A few hours later, a friend sent me a selfie. He’d just left the voting booth. His sticker was beautiful, tasteful, a testament to the subtle art of the “I Voted” sticker. A red ring enclosed a blue field. The crescent and palmetto (symbols of South Carolina) sat elegantly behind a bold white “I VOTED.”His sticker catches the eye. Passers-by will know exactly what the sticker says. They know he voted. Anyone looking at my sticker will wonder how I spilled some bronze paint on my chest. I trembled with indignation. One town over from me they’re giving out the good stickers and I’m stuck with slop. First my town of 12,000 installs 33 Flock cameras and now this? I spent some time scrolling through social media to see other “I Voted” stickers. So many are so beautiful. Michigan runs a contest where students can submit their own idea for a sticker and the state will print up the winners. , , and several other places around the country do the same. Louisiana commissions local artists to produce . My mouth hung up in a jealous scowl as I stared at pictures of New Orleanians bedecked with a sticker showing a hand drawn trumpet blasting out “I Voted” alongside Mardi Gras beads.Only Denton, Texas (another place I’ve lived, weirdly) seems to also have AI-generated slop stickers. Denton’s sticker is, at least, personalized. The city’s court house is in the corner looking more or less correct. The “I Voted” is large and centered in the sticker itself. Like mine, the image is too busy. Too much text, too many fireworks, and the inclusion of the Liberty Bell clutters the whole thing up. The central message — “I Voted” — is bright white. It doesn’t sink into a busy bronze soup like on my sticker.Complaining about AI-slop “I Voted” stickers may seem trivial in a world where AIs are choosing targets in warzones and vibecoders are every piece of software ever written. But these little things are important. These small annoyances pile up until things like are so ubiquitous that you don’t notice them anymore. The AI drive-thru and one day you stop worrying about it so much. You get an ugly AI slop “I Voted” sticker and you slap it on or toss it out. Enough of these build up until you don’t notice that AI all around you. And then, one day, it’s all normal.Right now we’re figuring out where our AI lines are. Society is negotiating what the future will look like. We’re , figuring out to keep our bosses happy, and learning what we will and won’t abide.Me? I draw the line at AI-generated “I Voted” stickers.

item.title: The Bull And Male Donkey Who Choose Each Other Again And Again (For Sex)
item.author: Sabrina Imbler
item.content:encoded: Elisabetta Palagi, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pisa, had sent her team of research students to Ethiopia to study geladas, monkeys whose hearts appear to gleam out of their chests. But as her students watched the geladas munch on a grassy plateau alongside other grazing animals, they noticed a peculiar interaction between two other animals. A bull approached a male donkey and mounted him. This behavior did not seem to bother the donkey. The donkey did not kick him or otherwise try to escape the interaction. The researchers contacted Palagi and asked if she thought this cross-species intercourse was worth studying. "I said yes," Palagi wrote in an email.After close observation, the researchers found that the the bull, dubbed Achille, and the donkey, dubbed Patroclo, have a persistent, mutual sexual relationship, which is described in a new paper in Achille and Patroclo's relationship was not news to the local herders, who laughed when they saw the researchers filming the unexpected pair. "What was an unexpected observation for us was evidently a familiar sight to them," Palagi said. (The paper includes explicit footage of the pair's mating that we have omitted out of respect for their privacy.)The plateau, with scattered gelada monkeys and Achille and Patroclo nuzzling on the left.

item.title: A Short Primer on Who Can ‘Seat’ Who and Other Post-Election Funny-Business
item.author: Josh Marshall
item.source: Josh Marshall – TPM – Talking Points Memo
item.content:encoded: First, the House and Senate are fundamentally different. The senate is a “continuing body”; so Republicans are in some position to refuse to seat Peltola. The House on the other hand reverts to what we might call a parliamentary state of nature every two years. When the House reconvenes in January, there won’t be a Republican majority and Mike Johnson will not be Speaker. Everyone shows up with their state certifications in hand and it’s the clerk of the House who examines those credentials on a ministerial basis. Then everyone votes on who the Speaker will be. That’s why we had that drama with Kevin McCarthy a few years ago.
